# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. - codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- copilot-fetch-x: Fetch the content of an X (Twitter) post using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares an x.com or twitter.com URL and wants its text or context. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-read-pdf: Extract the full text of a PDF as Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user wants to read, summarize, or quote a PDF file (in the vault or an absolute path). Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-web-fetch: Fetch and read the full contents of a specific web page (URL) as clean Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a link or asks you to open, read, or summarize a particular page — not for an open-ended web search. Requires an active Copilot Plus license; without it, use your own fetch tool instead.
- copilot-web-search: Search the web for current information using Copilot Plus. Use when the user asks to search online, look something up on the internet, or needs up-to-date facts beyond the vault. Prefer reading the vault for anything about the user's own notes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-youtube-transcript: Fetch the transcript of a YouTube video using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a YouTube URL and wants its contents, a summary, or quotes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- miyo-search: Semantic (meaning-based) search over the user's Obsidian vault via the local Miyo app. For any vault-search intent, use it when builtin grep search is too slow or doesn't surface enough relevant notes, or when the user explicitly asks for Miyo search. Needs the Miyo desktop app installed and running.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

346	**Purpose:** Edit, review, or refresh existing marketing copy through a seven-sweep framework (Clarity, Voice & Tone, So What, Prove It, Specificity, Heightened Emotion, Zero Risk) with optional expert-panel scoring for high-stakes pages. Not a rewriter — works existing draft toward publish-ready. When the copy is a Markdown file, delivers edits as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat suggestions are the fallback for pasted text.
347	**Triggers:** "edit this copy", "review my copy", "polish this", "copy sweep", "tighten this up", "proofread", "refresh this content", "content audit"
348	**File:** `Skills/Marketing/copy-editing/SKILL.md`

354	**File:** `Skills/Marketing/launch/SKILL.md`

365	**Triggers:** "marketing psychology", "mental models", "why people buy", "cognitive bias", "persuasion", "behavioral science"
366	**File:** `Skills/Marketing/marketing-psychology/SKILL.md`
367	**Dependencies:** None
368	
369	### Storybrand Messaging
370	**Purpose:** Diagnoses APR sales pages, email nurture sequences, and lead-magnet opt-ins against the StoryBrand SB7 narrative framework. Strict customer-as-hero mode. Output is suggestion-only and hybrid: the SB7 scorecard, diagnostic checks, and hero-violation flags stay in chat, while the 2-3 alternative phrasings for the weakest sections drop inline as CriticMarkup when the asset is a Markdown file (see criticmarkup-editing). Every alternative shows the stock StoryBrand version alongside an APR-voice-adjusted version (Mark chose this side-by-side mode). Does not propose alternatives to the canonical one-liner. Italicised passages in drafts are treated as Mark's author notes, not buyer copy. Distilled from the StoryBrand book; sits beside Marketing/copy-editing rather than replacing it (StoryBrand handles page-level narrative bones, copy-editing handles sentence-level tightening).
371	**Triggers:** "StoryBrand review", "SB7 review", "customer-as-hero check", "is this customer-focused", "is my sales page customer-focused", "review my sales page through StoryBrand", "review my nurture sequence", "review this opt-in", "brand script"

375	---
376	
377	## Adding or Changing a Skill
378	
379	Skills are the source of truth; this index is generated. To add one:
380	
381	1. Create `Skills/<Category>/<name>/SKILL.md` with the injected frontmatter keys (`name`, `category`, `triggered`, `triggers`, `purpose`, `dependencies`).

383	3. Append a build-log entry to `Skills/_build-log.md`.
384	
385	Run `python3 Skills/_gen_index.py --check` to confirm the index is in sync (used by the pre-commit hook).

## Routine Skills

### Quarterly Review
**Purpose:** A quarterly check-in workflow that reviews the calendar quarter Mark is closing out (calendar, email volume, completed work), rolls up quarter-level analytics and marketing experiments, surfaces a few Content Ideas, scans what's ahead, and produces a summary with priorities. Includes a read-only git work-recap across the APR repos (agile-pain-relief-astro, social-media-posting) summarizing what shipped, grouped by theme. The weekly review scaled to a quarter, but **read-only** - it deliberately omits the OmniFocus inbox sweep and the Drafts cleanup. In-chat only; never saved to a file; no reflective questions. LifeHQ-Mark is excluded by a global deny rule. Window defaults to the quarter being closed out (mid-quarter → quarter start through today; early in a new quarter → the full just-ended quarter).
**Triggers:** "quarterly review", "how'd my quarter go", "plan my quarter", "quarterly work summary", "what did I ship this quarter", "recap the quarter"
**File:** `Skills/Routines/quarterly-review/SKILL.md`

### Shutdown Routine

Includes a read-only git work-recap across the APR repos (agile-pain-relief-astro, social-media-posting) summarizing what shipped, grouped by theme. In-chat only -- never saved to a file; no reflective questions. LifeHQ-Mark is excluded by a global deny rule.
**Triggers:** "weekly review", "how'd my week go", "plan my week", "Sunday review", "what did I ship this week", "weekly work summary", "recap the repos"

## APR Skills

### Blog Critique
**Purpose:** Critiques a draft blog post against Mark's established writing style. Flags tone slips, off-voice vocabulary, and clunky sentence structures, plus a logic and content gap analysis and a dependency-order (information-DAG) check that section order grounds each term/concept before a later section leans on it. When a post mentions Scrum events, artifacts, or roles, fact-checks those claims against the current Scrum Guide and flags unintended deviations. No rewrites. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat bullets are the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "critique this blog post", "review my blog draft", "blog critique", "voice check my blog", "does this blog sound like me"
**File:** `Skills/APR/blog-critique/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

### Competitive Landscape
**Purpose:** Competitive analysis frameworks (Porter's Five Forces, Blue Ocean, positioning maps) tailored for APR's Scrum/Agile training and GenAI-for-business-agility market. Writes new analyses to `APR/Analytics/`.
**Triggers:** "analyze competitors", "competitive landscape", "identify differentiation", "market positioning", "Porter's Five Forces"
**File:** `Skills/APR/competitive-landscape/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Existing APR competitive docs in `APR/Analytics/` (e.g. `genai-course-competitive-analysis.md`)

### Content Performance
**Purpose:** Analyze APR content performance across social media, email newsletters, and website traffic. Reads raw data from the Astro repo (`agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/`), writes a single live snapshot to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` (overwrite, not dated).
**Triggers:** "content performance", "analyze my content", "how are my posts doing", "newsletter engagement", "which topics perform best", "social to website traffic"
**File:** `Skills/APR/content-performance/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Bash access to Astro repo analytics folder, `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` for matching newsletter content

### Linkedin Style
**Purpose:** Two modes for Mark's LinkedIn presence. Review mode (default) critiques draft posts against Mark's voice and LinkedIn-specific conventions (length, hooks, emoji, hashtags, external links), fact-checks any Scrum events/artifacts/roles against the current Scrum Guide, and delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup on a Markdown file (chat is the fallback for pasted text). Draft mode generates 2-3 complete draft-post options from a topic Mark gives or from his blog/glossary/newsletter content, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source so the draft already sounds like him and he can edit rather than start blank. Covers Scrum/Agile posts, GenAI/LLM posts (skeptical-pragmatist lean), personal posts, and business announcements.
**Triggers:** "review this LinkedIn post", "critique my post", "LinkedIn style", "LinkedIn rubric", "post review", "does this post sound like me", "voice check on this post", "draft a LinkedIn post", "give me LinkedIn post ideas", "draft LinkedIn options", "LinkedIn post from this newsletter", "draft some posts on"
**File:** `Skills/APR/linkedin-style/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format); reference newsletters in `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` optional for calibration; cross-platform emoji policy in `_social-posting-conventions.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo)

### Newsletter Reading Recap
**Purpose:** Builds the "Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole" section for the newsletter — a paste-ready Markdown list of what Mark read since the last issue, linked to originals, with neutral one-line descriptions. Papers and PDFs lead; archived-without-highlights items are demoted to a short trailing list. Window defaults to "since the last newsletter" (auto-detected from the Newsletter folder). Skips any article already featured in the reading section of the last 15 issues (exclusion set derived from the newsletter files themselves, reading-section links only, URL-normalized); the window can widen further back since repeats are filtered. Read-only and print-to-chat only; never edits the newsletter file.
**Triggers:** "reading recap for the newsletter", "reading rabbit hole", "what should go in the newsletter reading list", "newsletter reading section"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reading-recap/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Readwise CLI (preferred) or Readwise MCP; reads `Skills/Readwise/readwise-cli/SKILL.md` for command reference

### Newsletter Reviewer
**Purpose:** Reviews and critiques draft newsletters against Mark's authentic voice, tone, and style guidelines. Produces a structured critique with anti-pattern detections, terminology checks, a provisional subject-line check (filename-derived line plus any `// Subject A:` / `// Subject B:` A/B variants), a Scrum Guide accuracy fact-check when the draft mentions Scrum events/artifacts/roles, and priority fixes. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat critique is the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "review my newsletter", "critique this draft", "does this sound like me", "voice check", "newsletter rubric", "style check", "review my subject line", "subject line check"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

### Reshare Queue Tune
**Purpose:** Quarterly performance re-tier of the social-media reshare queue in `complete-social-media-calendar.md`. Measures how each already-posted queue item performed when reshared (PostHog `archive-reshare` attribution, LinkedIn-weighted, normalised to clicks-per-reshare) plus social engagement from `history.json`, then proposes tier moves (promote to TIER 2 / demote / retire) and surfaces high-traffic pages not yet queued. This is the **major** update; the monthly **minor** update (curate newly published posts/glossary via `calendar-audit`) does not need this skill. Approval gate before editing; refreshes the header with `calendar-audit --write`.
**Triggers:** "tune the reshare queue", "re-tier the calendar", "which reshares are working", "reshare queue review", "quarterly social queue update"
**File:** `Skills/APR/reshare-queue-tune/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `apr-weekly-analytics` (data refresh), `apr-content-performance` (optional context), `calendar-audit` in the `social-media-posting` repo, Bash access to Astro repo analytics; pairs with `quarterly-review`

### Seo Audit
**Purpose:** Diagnose structural SEO issues on agilepainrelief.com. Five-section audit framework (Crawlability, Technical, On-Page, Content/E-E-A-T, Authority) tightened for an Astro content/blog site. Produces a prioritised findings report at `APR/Analytics/seo-audit-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Findings only, no auto-fix.
**Triggers:** "audit my SEO", "SEO audit", "why am I not ranking", "SEO health check", "my traffic dropped", "check my technical SEO"
**File:** `Skills/APR/seo-audit/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Bash access to the Astro repo, latest GSC export (run the `Google Search Console Export` task in Operations first if stale), browser for PSI / Rich Results Test

### Weekly Analytics
**Purpose:** Orchestrate the weekly analytics loop — run `npm run scrape` and `npm run posthog-export` in the Astro repo, invoke `apr-content-performance` to regenerate the live report, flag experiment follow-ups, capture tasks to OmniFocus.
**Triggers:** "run weekly analytics", "refresh analytics", "pull analytics", "weekly data pull"
**File:** `Skills/APR/weekly-analytics/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `apr-content-performance`, `omnifocus-capture`, `omnifocus-workflow`, Bash access to Astro repo

---

## Writing Skills

### Criticmarkup Editing
**Purpose:** Default delivery format for feedback on Mark's Markdown writing -- annotate the file in place with CriticMarkup (comments `{>>Claude: …<<}`, additions `{++…++}`, deletions `{--…--}`, substitutions `{~~old~>new~~}`, highlights `{==…==}`), reviewed in Obsidian's Track Changes side panel. The voice rubrics decide WHAT to flag; this skill decides HOW to deliver it. Always delivers the full markup pass in one go (no section-by-section chunking; the CLAUDE.md chunked-review preference does not apply to CriticMarkup passes). Applies to all writing types including sales/marketing copy. Never rewrites Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper. Falls back to chat bullets for pasted (non-file) content.
**Triggers:** "edit this", "mark up my draft", "track changes", "use CriticMarkup", "suggest edits inline", "give me feedback on my writing"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Obsidian Track Changes plugin (`.obsidian/plugins/track-changes/`); read alongside the relevant voice rubric (apr-blog-critique, apr-newsletter-reviewer, apr-linkedin-style, Marketing/copy-editing, storybrand-messaging)

### Email Voice
**Purpose:** Mark's email writing voice, for a dictation tool to draft emails that sound like him. Covers shared structure, professional vs personal registers, mechanics, and a dictation correction/vocabulary list. Built from analysis of 50+ sent emails.
**Triggers:** "draft an email", "write this email in my voice", "email in my voice", "make this email sound like me", "reply to this email as me"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/email-voice/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** None

---

## Communication Skills

### Drafts Inbox
**Purpose:** Triages everything in the Drafts inbox (no longer keyed to a "cowork" tag), classifies each item, takes action, and archives when done so the inbox stays the unprocessed queue. For a large backlog, asks how far back to go and filters by `modificationDate`. Tasks route to `omnifocus-capture`.
**Triggers:** "check my Drafts inbox", "process my inbox", "what's in Drafts", "triage my Drafts inbox", "drafts inbox triage"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/drafts-inbox/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Drafts MCP connector; `Skills/OmniFocus/capture/SKILL.md` (for task capture)

### Gmail Triage
**Purpose:** Recommend a triage plan for the Gmail inbox via the Gmail MCP. Classifies each thread into one of four actions — reference (file under existing label), reply-needed (draft suggestion only), trash, or archive (remove INBOX, keep in All Mail for records) — with a Task overlay for emails that imply an OmniFocus action. All recommendations require explicit per-item approval, presented in batches of 10. Replies handled in a separate pass. Only uses existing labels; never creates new ones. Trashing uses the Gmail TRASH label (30-day recovery). Sender-specific rules and aging rules live in `memory/feedback_gmail_triage.md`. Task captures delegate to `omnifocus-capture`.
**Triggers:** "triage my Gmail", "process my Gmail inbox", "Gmail triage", "sort my Gmail", "Gmail inbox zero"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/gmail-triage/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Gmail MCP connector (authenticated), `Skills/OmniFocus/capture/SKILL.md` (for Task overlay), `memory/feedback_gmail_triage.md` (sender rules)

### Growthmaterial Export
**Purpose:** Export emails labelled `Courses and Memberships/GrowthMaterial` to Markdown under `~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/3 - YFL/14 - TRAININGS & BIZ DEV/GrowthInReverse/Emails/`. ## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

1	# Social posts — week of 2026-07-14 (next-few-days batch)
2	
3	Working draft, rebuilt under the updated linkedin-style rules: each draft is a re-cut of your own sentences from the source blog/glossary/newsletter (lifted close to verbatim, lightly stitched), in connected prose rather than punchy fragments, at the fuller current length. **Pick one option per item, tweak in your own voice, then tell me and I'll build the 3-platform batch JSON** at `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/next-few-days.json`, condensing each to LinkedIn / Mastodon (<=500) / Bluesky (<=290).
4	
5	Conventions when I build the JSON: the URL goes in the `url` field (no UTM, no inline links; the pipeline adds per-platform UTM), and `image` stays `""` (the pipeline scrapes og:image).
6	
7	**Selection (all `[ ]` in the queue):**
8	- Blog — GenAI Code Quality: Fundamental Flaws and Bluffing (TIER 1)
9	- Blog — The Sprint Backlog: Complete Guide (TIER 2)
10	- Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy (TIER 1)
11	- Glossary — Definition of Done

16	## 1. Blog — GenAI code quality / bluffing
17	**URL:** /blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/
18	
19	### Option A — the data, and why it's structural
20	AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues, and the GenAI code quality gap is turning into a chasm. That's not a random number, it's from a CodeRabbit research report, which also shows 30-41% more tech debt and 39% more cognitive complexity.
21	
22	These problems are structural. They don't magically fix themselves, when Anthropic releases a new model. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Some teams think TDD is the fix, and others suggest we can code review our way out of this. We can't code review our way out of this mess, because that just puts the burden on humans to tidy up the mess that the AI created.
23	
24	So instead of trying to build quality into code faster, why don't we work on making sure we know what the right product is first? When it comes to the code itself, give the models smaller, more focused tasks, and start with a small set of acceptance criteria for a single feature.
25	
26	What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.
27	
28	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
29	
30	### Option B — the bluffing
31	GenAI code quality problems start with how the models are trained. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Worse, 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the models learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses.
32	
33	OX Security likens this to an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment. So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. It forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution, but it can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste.
34	
35	The next release from Anthropic/OpenAI won't magically solve the problem. The labs aren't prioritizing: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Until that changes, we deal with what we've got, one small and focused task at a time.
36	
37	What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.
38	
39	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile
40	
41	---
42	
43	## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
44	**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/
45	
46	### Option A — ownership
47	Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement, because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something that they choose.
48	
49	Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it, not a tool, and not an outsider. Many teams also benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress. Teams that limit WIP to two or three Product Backlog Items tend to collaborate more, cross-skill faster, and eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint.
50	
51	Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make it even better.
52	
53	#Scrum #ScrumMaster
54	
55	### Option B — anti-patterns
56	Sprint Backlog's are Scrum's most misunderstood artifact. They're not a list of tickets or tasks. (thanks JIRA.) They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.
57	
58	When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.
59	
60	The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.
61	
62	Which Sprint Backlog anti-pattern have you seen the most?
63	
64	#Scrum #ProductOwner
65	
66	---
67	
68	## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy
69	**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/
70	
71	### Option A — the knowledge cliff
72	We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future.
73	
74	When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill, and this affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.
75	
76	NASA has been through this recently. They want to build big rockets again, and they have mountains of documentation, literally 2900 cubic feet, but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it. This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one.
77	
78	So before automating with AI, ask: do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
79	
80	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership
81	
82	### Option B — pilots and radiologists
83	In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.
84	
85	In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.
86	
87	Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.
88	
89	Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
90	
91	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
92	
93	---
94	
95	## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
96	**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/
97	
98	### Option A — the pressure
99	The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.
100	
101	The hardest problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features. As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt, making future work slower and more error-prone.
102	
103	That's why the team need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done, and only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.
104	
105	#Scrum #ScrumMaster
106	
107	### Option B — undone work
108	When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It's a problem because it reduces transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories, yet the work isn't complete.
109	
110	Here's how that plays out later: a bug is found several Sprints after the code is written, and now new code relies on the defective behaviour. Or, missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.
111	
112	One caution: Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they're creating. It's not a reporting standard, and using it as one leads to micro management.
113	
114	#Scrum #ProductOwner
115	
116	---
117	
118	## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
119	**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
120	*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*
121	
122	### Option A — 5% vs 20%
123	By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action.
124	
125	I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, which I read on a hiking trip in the Canary Islands that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint, and Backlog Refinement takes up another 3-5%. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.
126	
127	When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced, and now I have research to support it.
128	
129	#Scrum #Agile
130	
131	### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
132	Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning.
133	
134	By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans, when the research suggests it should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. Scrum already builds that in: Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are all about planning and goal attainment, and Backlog Refinement adds a little more.
135	
136	As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output.
137	
138	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

GenAI code quality problems start with how the models are trained. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Worse, 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the models learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses.

OX Security likens this to an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment. So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. It forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution, but it can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste.

The next release from Anthropic/OpenAI won't magically solve the problem. The labs aren't prioritizing: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Until that changes, we deal with what we've got, one small and focused task at a time.

What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile

---

## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/

### Option A — ownership
Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement, because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something that they choose.

Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it, not a tool, and not an outsider. Many teams also benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress. Teams that limit WIP to two or three Product Backlog Items tend to collaborate more, cross-skill faster, and eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint.

Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make it even better.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — anti-patterns
Sprint Backlog's are Scrum's most misunderstood artifact. They're not a list of tickets or tasks. (thanks JIRA.) They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.

Which Sprint Backlog anti-pattern have you seen the most?

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy
**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/

### Option A — the knowledge cliff
We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future.

When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill, and this affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.

NASA has been through this recently. They want to build big rockets again, and they have mountains of documentation, literally 2900 cubic feet, but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it. This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one.

So before automating with AI, ask: do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

### Option B — pilots and radiologists
In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.

In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.

Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.

Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/

### Option A — the pressure
The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.

The hardest problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features. As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt, making future work slower and more error-prone.

That's why the team need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done, and only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — undone work
When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It's a problem because it reduces transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories, yet the work isn't complete.

Here's how that plays out later: a bug is found several Sprints after the code is written, and now new code relies on the defective behaviour. Or, missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.

One caution: Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they're creating. It's not a reporting standard, and using it as one leads to micro management.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*

### Option A — 5% vs 20%
By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action.

I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, which I read on a hiking trip in the Canary Islands that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint, and Backlog Refinement takes up another 3-5%. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.

When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced, and now I have research to support it.

#Scrum #Agile

### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning.

By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans, when the research suggests it should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. Scrum already builds that in: Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are all about planning and goal attainment, and Backlog Refinement adds a little more.

As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

==== ITEM 0 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/
image: 
-- linkedin --
🇨🇦 Canada has a real productivity problem, and we have for decades. In 1984 the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked; by 2022 it had fallen to 71%. The new national AI strategy is an attempt to fix that, promising a 3 percent increase in GDP by raising business adoption of GenAI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034.

Here's my worry: adoption of GenAI doesn't make an organization more productive. Dropping GenAI onto a broken process just automates the mess. Worse, a target like this invites AI washing, because when you measure success by adoption rate, organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks, and focus on eliminating the bottleneck.

What would it take for your organization to measure the outcome instead of the adoption rate?

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

To improve productivity, treat each organization as a system and eliminate the bottleneck.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
-- bluesky --
🇨🇦 Adoption isn't productivity. Dropping GenAI on a broken process just automates the mess. Fix the bottleneck, not the adoption rate.

==== ITEM 1 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/product-backlog/
image: 
-- linkedin --
📋 The Product Backlog is an ordered list of all the work items or value the Product Owner would like to see the team work on in the foreseeable future. Simple enough as a definition. The trouble starts when it stops being ordered and turns into a dumping ground.

An ordered list means someone has decided what matters most, and the team pulls from the top. When everything is "high priority", nothing is, and the list quietly becomes a graveyard of ideas nobody will ever build. A deep backlog isn't a full one; it's one that's well understood near the top and deliberately vague further down, because refining work you may never do is waste.

If your Product Backlog has hundreds of items and no clear order, that's not thoroughness. It's a decision nobody has made yet.

How many items are really in your Product Backlog, and when did you last delete one?

#Scrum #ProductOwner
-- mastodon --
📋 The Product Backlog is an ordered list of the work the Product Owner wants the team to tackle next. The trouble starts when it stops being ordered and turns into a dumping ground.

When everything is "high priority", nothing is, and the list becomes a graveyard of ideas nobody will build. A deep backlog is well understood near the top and deliberately vague further down.

When did you last delete a backlog item?

#Scrum #ProductOwner
-- bluesky --
📋 A Product Backlog is an ordered list. When everything is "high priority", nothing is, and it becomes a graveyard nobody will build. When did you last delete one?

==== ITEM 2 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/
image: 
-- linkedin --
🔄 A senior architect is trapped in what he calls a "vicious death spiral." His Scrum Master decided to split the work: one team handles user stories while another manages technical integrations. Six sprints in, refinement and planning sessions routinely exceed eight hours. Stories arrive incomplete, missing critical integration details. Dependencies bounce between groups, estimates become guesswork, and team members mentally check out around hour five.

A problem like this is exactly where I'd reach for Systems Thinking, a mental model that views problems as interconnected parts rather than isolated issues. The trouble is that it's hard to keep the questions in mind while exploring a problem. I've been using Systems Thinking as a lens for years, and I still forget to ask some of them. So this time I used GenAI as a sparring partner.

When I explained that everyone says the split is just more efficient, and that they're measuring how much work each person gets done, the model named it: a classic systems thinking trap called local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization is measuring output (how busy each specialist is) but not outcome (how quickly customer value flows through the system).

The most insightful element of the whole exchange: the system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem. The Scrum Master keeps extending sessions, believing more time will surface all hidden complexity, while the architect has watched the same story carry over three sprints because the slicing never works.

When your team keeps carrying the same story across sprints, ask whether you're solving a structure problem with a process problem.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
-- mastodon --
🔄 A senior architect calls his project a "vicious death spiral." Work was split: one team on stories, another on integrations. Six sprints in, planning drags and stories arrive incomplete.

I used GenAI as a Systems Thinking sparring partner. Everyone said the split was "more efficient", measuring output, not outcome. A classic local-optimization trap.

The system keeps solving a structure problem with a process problem.
-- bluesky --
🔄 A split team (stories vs integrations) in a "death spiral." GenAI as a Systems Thinking partner named the trap: measuring output, not outcome.

==== ITEM 3 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/definition-of-ready/
image: 
-- linkedin --
🚦 Most teams treat Definition of Ready as a checklist to enforce. I'd rather you hold it lightly.

If items frequently get stuck mid-Sprint because something was ill-understood, a Definition of Ready can help, but only cover the details that are actually causing problems right now. Instead of "all acceptance criteria", try "some or enough acceptance criteria have been found". Instead of "requires a mockup", try "features that need large UI changes check whether a mockup would help, preferring pencil sketches".

Then, as the team matures, check whether the Definition of Ready can be made thinner by reducing the number of elements in it. The failure mode to watch for is that it becomes a dumping ground for every little problem the team ever had. A lightweight check is a tool for good; a rigid gate that everything must 100% comply with is how you end up optimizing for looking productive instead of being useful.

Does your "Ready" gate reduce delay, or just hide it earlier in the process?

#Scrum #ScrumMaster
-- mastodon --
🚦 Most teams treat Definition of Ready as a checklist to enforce. Hold it lightly instead.

If items get stuck mid-Sprint, a Definition of Ready can help, but only cover the details actually causing problems now. As the team matures, make it thinner. The failure mode: it becomes a dumping ground for every little problem the team ever had.

Does your "Ready" gate reduce delay, or just hide it earlier?

#Scrum #ScrumMaster
-- bluesky --
🚦 Treat Definition of Ready as a rigid checklist and it becomes a dumping ground for every past problem. Hold it lightly: cover only what's causing trouble now.

==== ITEM 4 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/team-friction-inspires-working-agreements/
image: 
-- linkedin --
🤝 When a team decides to build a Working Agreement, the ScrumMaster's job is to coach, not lead. As usual for a ScrumMaster, good preparation pays dividends, so canvass the team beforehand about the categories that matter: Daily Scrum start time, respect, phone usage in team events, how to give everyone an equal voice.

Start with a check-in, the same as you would in a Retrospective, so people get a chance to say where their head and heart are before the work begins. Then use a format that guarantees every voice is heard. I like the 1-2-4 model: each person shares their ideas, pairs record the best ones, then small groups consolidate and bring proposals back to the whole. Use the Decider Protocol to check for consensus quickly, and when someone says no, they're expected to suggest something better.

Here's what one fictional team landed on: don't interrupt, and reflect back your understanding before responding. More vocal members volunteer to speak last. At least one person volunteers to be the dissenter, expected to find criticisms of an idea with the goal of making it stronger.

Every few Sprints, ask in a Retrospective: is this still our Working Agreement, and what would we like to change?

#Scrum #ScrumMaster
-- mastodon --
🤝 Building a Working Agreement? The ScrumMaster coaches, not leads. Canvass the team first on what matters: Daily Scrum time, respect, phones, equal voice.

Start with a check-in, then use a format where every voice is heard (I like 1-2-4 with the Decider Protocol). When someone says no, they suggest something better.

Every few Sprints, ask: is this still our Working Agreement?

#Scrum #ScrumMaster
-- bluesky --
🤝 Building a Working Agreement? The ScrumMaster coaches, not leads. Use a format where every voice is heard, and revisit it every few Sprints.

==== ITEM 5 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/product-backlog-refinement/
image: 
-- linkedin --
🗂️ Product Backlog Refinement (once called "grooming") is the session where the whole Scrum Team prepares the Product Backlog for the next few Sprints. New items get added, items too large for one Sprint get broken down, the Product Owner shares the reasoning behind prioritization decisions, and items that no longer matter get deleted to make room.

Notice how much of that is conversation, not paperwork. The value isn't a tidy backlog; it's the shared understanding the team builds while getting there. That's also why I don't think GenAI will speed this event up, and shouldn't. The point of refinement is that a group reaches a common understanding of the work, and you can't outsource that to a tool without losing the very thing you came for.

Which part of refinement does your team treat as paperwork, when it should be a conversation?

#Scrum
-- mastodon --
🗂️ Product Backlog Refinement is where the whole Scrum Team prepares the backlog for the next few Sprints: adding items, breaking down big ones, sharing prioritization reasoning, deleting what no longer matters.

Most of that is conversation, not paperwork. The value is the shared understanding. That's why GenAI won't speed it up, and shouldn't.

What does your team treat as paperwork here?

#Scrum
-- bluesky --
🗂️ Product Backlog Refinement isn't paperwork; it's where the team builds shared understanding. That's why GenAI won't speed it up, and shouldn't.

==== ITEM 6 ====
url: https://agilepainrelief.com/newsletter-subscribe/
image: 
-- linkedin --

🔄 A senior architect is trapped in what he calls a "vicious death spiral." His Scrum Master decided to split the work: one team handles user stories while another manages technical integrations. A problem like this is exactly where I'd reach for Systems Thinking, a mental model that views problems as interconnected parts rather than isolated issues. The trouble is that it's hard to keep the questions in mind while exploring a problem. I've been using Systems Thinking as a lens for years, and I still forget to ask some of them. So this time I used GenAI as a sparring partner.

When I explained that everyone says the split is just more efficient, and that they're measuring how much work each person gets done, the model named it: a classic systems thinking trap called local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization is measuring output (how busy each specialist is) but not outcome (how quickly customer value flows through the system).

**Product Backlog Refinement** (formerly known as "Product Backlog Grooming") is a session during which the Scrum Team (Developers, Product Owner, ScrumMaster) prepare the Product Backlog for the next few sprints. **Definition of Ready** is an agreement between the Product Owner and the team that describes what state Product Backlog Items (or User Stories) need to be in before the Sprint. Another way of describing “ready” is how prepared Stories are to be worked on.

A Definition of Ready helps a Scrum (or Kanban) team to ensure that their Product Backlog Items are well thought out, so nothing is considered for Sprint work if it has a high risk of getting stuck because some part of the work was ill-understood.

Here are some elements commonly found in a Definition of Ready:

- Clear Understanding. Everyone agrees on what each Backlog Item represents.
- Estimated and Small. The item has an estimate and it is, at most, a Small or 1, 2, 3 Story Points.
- Acceptance Criteria. All acceptance criteria has been defined.
- Dependencies. All dependencies have been discovered.
- User Interface. A feature requires a mockup.

This list has strong parallels to the INVEST criteria and, as long as it remains a lightweight check, Definition of Ready can be a tool for good.

A team with a Definition of Ready isn’t optimizing for getting an idea from entering the Product Backlog to Deployed. Instead, they’re optimizing for Sprint Backlog to Deployed. The Definition of Ready acts a gate between the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Items can be held up at the gate for trivial reasons (e.g. incomplete Acceptance Criteria, missing user interface mockup, etc).

<Figure
  src={DefinitionOfReadyHarmfulHelpfulExamples1024x538}
  alt="Scrum Definition of Ready - harmful and helpful examples"
  caption="Scrum Definition of Ready - harmful and helpful examples"
/>


A rigid Definition of Ready encourages local optimization for the throughput of just the Scrum Team. This sounds like a more positive thing than it really is. The problem is that we should be optimizing for the whole system from the moment the customer places asks for their feature, until it is delivered. A rigid “Ready”, makes the Scrum Team look better by improving their cycle time, without necessarily improving things for the client. Imagine an example where a Definition of Ready holds up a feature for 6+ weeks while requirements are being gathered (perhaps the User Interface details, or final Acceptance criteria). Sure, once the work starts, it proceeds at a normal pace, but now the Scrum Team can say that they’ve reduced their cycle time, when all that really happened is the delay was pushed to early in the system. The team feels good but the customer isn't any happier. The customer's item still spent a long time sitting in a queue, and it doesn't matter what the queue was.

For teams that use a Definition of Ready, they should consider measuring Lead Time and not Cycle Time. By measuring Lead Time, any time spent waiting at the Ready gate is accounted for, making it harder to sub-optimize. This also leads to a general principle that says, when measuring, prefer measurements that observe the whole system.

  src={LeadTimeCycleTimeKanbanBoardExample}

/>

date: '2026-02-05'

import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';

The **Last Responsible Moment** sounds like a fancy name for procrastination, though it isn't. Instead of procrastination, it's about remaining flexible and deciding when we have more information.

A useful framing: think about how much more you'll know about a problem or decision in the future. Is the person sitting here now the same person six weeks from now? Of course, the answer is "future me" will know more. So why lock in a decision today when future-you will be better equipped to make it?

With the Last Responsible Moment, we delay decisions until the cost of not deciding exceeds the benefit of delaying. When we make a decision too early, we bake in the assumptions we were making at the time. When we delay too long, we lose the ability to make the decision altogether.

A practical approach when facing a decision:
- When is the last time I could make this decision?
- What would I need to know before I make this decision?

This idea appears throughout the Agile Universe, even when we don't name it. All Agile Engineering Practices are about avoiding early decisions. In Product Backlog Refinement, we encourage teams only to refine a few Sprints' worth of work. The list goes on.

The idea of the Last Responsible Moment came to the Agile community via Mary and Tom Poppendieck's *Lean Software Development: An Agile Toolkit*:

> Delay commitment until the last responsible moment, that is, the moment at which failing to make a decision eliminates an important alternative.

Not everyone loves the framing: Rebecca Wirfs-Brock argues that we should decide at the “most responsible moment”, the point where we know enough to choose well, rather than nervously delaying until an alternative is about to disappear (see Resource Links below).

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';

**Product Backlog Refinement** (formerly known as "Product Backlog Grooming") is a session during which the Scrum Team (Developers, Product Owner, ScrumMaster) prepare the Product Backlog for the next few sprints. New Product Backlog Items (PBIs) are added for new needs to be considered. PBIs that are too large to be worked on in a single Sprint are broken down into smaller items. Estimates are made as to how much time each PBI will require to complete. The Product Owner makes prioritization decisions about PBIs, sharing with the Team their reasoning. PBIs that are no longer important are deleted, making room for new ones. The items that are candidates for the next Sprint Planning have their initial acceptance criteria written.

---
title: 'Scrum by Example - Team Friction Inspires Working Agreements'
date: '2023-11-23'
lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
categories:
