1	---
2	title: "What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size?"
3	date: "2020-03-13"
4	lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
5	categories:
6	  - 'team-dynamics-and-people'
7	coverImage: "@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v2-A.jpg"
8	excerpt: 'Discover the optimal Scrum team size based on research and 20+ years experience. Learn why 4-6 members works best, plus factors affecting team performance.'
9	---
10	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
11	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
12	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
13	import APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV2A from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v2-A.jpg';
14	import TeamSize from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/team-size.jpg';
15	import ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage1 from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Parallelizable-vs-Serial-Work-image-1.jpg';
16	import ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage3Equation from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Parallelizable-vs-Serial-Work-image-3-equation.jpg';
17	import ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage2 from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Parallelizable-vs-Serial-Work-image-2.jpg';
18	import AmdahlsLawGraph from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Amdahls-Law-graph.jpg';
19	import SociometryGroupSize from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Sociometry-group-size.jpg';
20	import PutnamMyersStudyPersonMonths from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Putnam-Myers-study-person-months.jpg';
21	import LarryMaccheroneTeamSizeToPerformance from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Larry-Maccherone-team-size-to-performance.png';
22	import APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV1B from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v1-B.jpg';
23	
24	Nearly every client I work with asks me this question: 'What's the optimal Scrum team size?' The [Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#team-dev) offers very limited guidance, suggesting 3-9 people per team (exclusive of ScrumMaster and Product Owner), without giving reasons or context for those numbers. The research and 20+ years of experience reveal a more nuanced answer that could dramatically impact your team's productivity.
25	
26	In many cases this question comes up as a side effect of [Sprint Planning from Hell](/blog/sprint-planning-from-hell/) or [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/) that goes on too long.
27	
28	There isn't one universally correct answer for optimal team size, but there are a number of factors and trade-offs worth considering when figuring out what will work best for your team.
29	
30	In this post, we'll explore the research, and I'll share my personal experiences about effective team size. While this is primarily about Scrum, the lessons are applicable for any work that is collaborative and knowledge-based.
31	
32	<Figure
33	  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV2A}
34	  alt="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
35	  caption="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
36	/>
37	
38	<CalloutBox heading="Key Takeaways: Optimal Scrum Team Size">
39	- **Best size**: There is no best size. However teams of 4-6 or often a good choice
40	- **Communication cost**: Relationships grow exponentially (N(N-1)/2 formula)
41	- **Avoid**: Teams of 8+ show diminishing returns
42	- **Critical factors**: Skills, stability of membership, and psychological safety matter as much as size
43	- **Evidence**: Multiple studies support smaller teams for knowledge work
44	</CalloutBox>
45	
46	## Effective Scrum Team Size is More than Just a Number
47	When you're trying to determine what will work best, your  Team's needs should be more important than any arbitrary number. Factors you should consider include:
48	
49	- A [sufficiently broad set of skills](/blog/how-to-cross-skill-and-grow-t-shaped-team-members/) to build their product – aka Cross-Functional
50	- Team members dedicated to one, and only one, team
51	- [Stable membership](/blog/stable-teams-really-do-matter/) – i.e. team membership that is consistent over a long period of time[^1]
52	- Diversity of thought – a sufficiently broad set of beliefs, attitudes and thinking patterns[^2]
53	
54	Once the Team is formed, these are often just as important as team size when predicting success:
55	
56	- Psychological safety – the environment is safe for all team members to share their ideas[^3][^4]
57	- Collective Intelligence of the Team – strongly correlated with average sensitivity of team members[^4]
58	- Equal Communication – the most expressive team member is no more than twice as expressive as the quietest[^5]
59	- Open-Mindedness and Willingness to Learn[^6]
60	- A Shared Vision of which all Team members are committed to achieving[^8]
61	- Clear Roles and Responsibilities[^9]
62	- Dynamically Shared Leadership[^10]
63	- External Coach – in Scrum this is the ScrumMaster
64	
65	These factors don't exist in a void, so let's explore the evidence that supports what others, including myself, have discovered about team size, to help you consider what's most important for your Team. After all, there is no universal answer, there is only a range that will likely work best for your needs.
66	
67	## The Problem with Arbitrary Numbers for Optimal Team Size
68	The earliest Scrum and XP books all suggest a team size number of 7+/-2, applying Miller's number,[^11] believed to be the number of integers you can hold in short-term memory. I'm troubled by this, since I can't see why one's ability to keep track of numbers should be correlated with team size. In addition, more recent research[^12] has shown that, as the things you're keeping track of become more complex, the number of items you can keep in your short-term memory drops to 4 or less. Clearly, we need more useful sources.
69	
70	Many other coaches cite historical examples going back to the Roman army, which used small military unit sizes of around 8 people. Others observe bonobos, one of the closest genetic relatives to humans, often split into groups of 6-7 to forage for a day. Both of these conveniently support the 7+/-2 number, but since neither example is about teams doing knowledge work, the relevance of these for Scrum is limited.
71	
72	## What Happens to Relationships When Teams Get Large?
73	<Figure
74	  src={TeamSize}
75	  alt="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
76	  caption="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
77	/>
78	
79	In a team, each individual will connect with another individual and form a unique relationship. The bigger the team, the more the relationships. The equation that describes this is N (N – 1)/2. But what exactly does that _mean_? More importantly, how is it supposed to help you? Let's start by treating it as a high-school math problem, then turn it into something we can actually use in real life.
80	
81	The above equation tells us how many different relationships will exist within a team of a certain size. N = the number of people in the team. So, in the first example of a team of 5 people, for N=5 you have 10 relationships: 10 different combinations of team members relating with other team members.
82	
83	In the second example, n=7, you have 21 relationships, and at n=9 in the third image you have 36 relationships.  Each pair of people represents one relationship, and that relationship is how they collaborate. High-performing teams, by their nature, must have strong relationships between each of the team members to collaborative effectively.
84	
85	Why does this matter, and how can it help you? Each new person adds some individual productivity to the Team, but they also increase the communications overhead in the form of an exponentially growing number of relationships. To increase a team from 5 to 7 people, you have to more than double the number of relationships. To go from 7 to 9, you don't quite double it, but the jump is still large.
86	
87	Just how expensive is it to maintain these relationships? Anecdotally, having studied team member interactions at clients' sites, I can say that in teams of 7-8 people, upwards of 90 minutes per person each day is spent interacting with other team members.[^13] This excludes pair programming time. Some of the interaction is talking about work, but just as much is spent socializing. This is good and important because it's the combination of work and socializing that builds a team's resilience and ability to handle challenges effectively (see the water cooler section in "[Five Steps Towards Creating High-Performance Teams](/learn/)").
88	
89	So the number of relationships between team members, and the time investment they require, needs to be a factor considered when choosing team size because it will influence productivity.
90	
91	A general rule of thumb suggests that people typically have from 3½ to 5 hours of productive time at work each day. As a team gets larger, we either lose productivity or, more often, we start to withdraw socially rather than sacrifice productive time for interacting with our peers because the communication costs for each team member is becoming too high to afford. We need strong relationships to become a high-performing team but, as group size grows, we start to avoid the interactions that build those relationships.[^14]
92	
93	### Many Hands Make Light Work… But Only to a Point
94	We all want to believe that if we go from 1 person to 2 people, or from 2 to 4 people, we will get a doubling of the amount of work done. Yet, we know intuitively that isn't the case.
95	
96	What we're missing is _why_. Enter "[Amdahl's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)." The formula, first presented in 1967, estimates how much of a speedup might be gained if we took a computing task and ran parts of it in parallel. If that sounds like gobbledygook, it just means sometimes programs have parts that can be worked on by multiple processors at the same time (i.e. parallel processing), but other parts that must be done one at a time (i.e. serial programming).
97	
98	<Figure
99	  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage1}
100	  alt="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
101	  caption="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
102	/>
103	
104	The first picture imagines work done by one processor. It takes 5 units of time.
105	
106	If we take the 5 units of work and apply 3 processors to the parts that can be done concurrently (parallel), it doesn't take 1 and 2/3 units of time (5 divided by 3) to complete. Instead, it takes 3 units because 2 of the units of work can only be done by one processor (serial). It's certainly an improvement in time, but not as much as you might expect.
107	
108	The math to explain the problem might look intimidating at first:
109	
110	<Figure
111	  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage3Equation}
112	  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
113	  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
114	/>
115	
116	
117	<Figure
118	  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage2}
119	  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
120	  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
121	/>
122	
123	Work in teams has similar properties. In fact, if we turn it into a graph, we see just how inefficient increased team size can be:
124	
125	<Figure
126	  src={AmdahlsLawGraph}
127	  alt="Amdahl's Law graph."
128	  caption="Amdahl's Law graph."
129	/>
130	
131	Just focus for now on the 80% line (teal, at the top) of the graph. Let's be optimistic (and unrealistic) and assume that 80% of the work can be done by working in parallel. This suggests that the more people doing it, the faster it will get done – right?  Ah, but wait. If we go from 1 person to 2 people, we don't get twice as much done. To get a 2 times improvement in work completed, we actually need 3 people. 7 people only create a 3.2 times improvement over 1 person. To get 4 times as much work done as 1 person, we would need 16 people!
132	
133	What happens if even less of the work can be done concurrently (parallel)? What if 50% of the work must be done in serial (red line on the graph)? Then with 9 people, we still have only a 1.8 times speedup.
134	
135	What's the solution? There's no easy fix, but there are things you can do to mitigate the effect of Amdahl's Law:
136	
137	- Make it so as much of the work as possible can be done in parallel. This may mean increasing cross-skilling and collaboration.
138	- Reduce cross-team dependencies, so there are no bottlenecks and delays.
139	- Increase the speed of the work process overall by improving quality and practices.
140	
141	Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from [building a high-performance team](/learn/) that is an optimal size for effectiveness, communication, and quality.
142	
143	## Research-Backed Evidence on Team Size
144	The American Sociological Association published a study by Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ on the "Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions."[^15]
145	
146	<Figure
147	  src={SociometryGroupSize}
148	  alt="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
149	  caption="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
150	/>
151	
152	In this study, they had participants complete a number of tasks – a mix of Production (writing), Discussion, and Problem-Solving. The participants were placed in different groups sized from 2 to 7. After completing each task, volunteers were asked a number of questions, including two that this graph displays: "was your group too small?", "was your group too large?". As you can see from the graph, groups around 4-5 in size seemed to have the least negative reaction. The oft-cited number is 4.6. The participants were undergraduate students (all men, sadly), the tasks had a cognitive load but were not programming, and the groups weren't together long enough for a real sense of a "team" to form. Nonetheless, it is an interesting data point.
153	
154	By the time Hackman wrote the book _Leading Teams_, his rule of thumb for team size was 6.
155	
156	Jennifer Mueller cited in "[Is Your Team Too Big? Too Small? What's the Right Number?](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/is-your-team-too-big-too-small-whats-the-right-number-2/):"
157	
158	> _if companies are dealing with coordination tasks and motivational issues, and you ask, 'What is your team size and what is optimal?' that correlates to a team of six. "Above and beyond five, and you begin to see diminishing motivation," says Mueller. "After the fifth person, you look for cliques. And the number of people who speak at any one time? That's harder to manage in a group of five or more."_
159	
160	It's not just personal opinions from team members that teach us about optimal group size: we also have objective statistics. Putnam and Myers surveyed data from 491 software projects in a large corporation.[^16] These were projects with 35,000 – 90,000 source lines of code. They broke projects down into buckets based on the number of people involved in the project: 1.5-3, 3-5, 5-7, 9-11, and 15-20. On average, the smaller groups (3-5, 5-7) took significantly less time (11.9 and 11.6 months, respectively) than the larger groups (17.1 and 16.29 months) to complete similar-sized projects.
161	
162	When you multiply the number of team members times the number of months, you get a graph that is even more shocking:
163	
164	<Figure
165	  src={PutnamMyersStudyPersonMonths}
166	  alt="Putnam Myers study graph. "
167	  caption="Putnam Myers study graph. "
168	/>
169	
170	A team of 9-11 people took  around2.5-3.5 times as long as teams of 5-7 and 3-5 to complete projects of a similar size. That suggests that teams larger than seven in this dataset were just a way to spend money faster because of the increased team size but reduced net performance.
171	
172	## Evidence from Agile Projects
173	Larry Maccherone, in his work through both Rally, Tasktop, and AgileCraft, has helped build large datasets about practices in Agile Teams. His data shows:
174	
175	<Figure
176	  src={LarryMaccheroneTeamSizeToPerformance}
177	  alt="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
178	  caption="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
179	/>
180	
181	Based on Larry's data, it would appear that teams of 1-3 are more productive but have lower quality. Teams of 3-5 are marginally more productive than 5-9, although they might still have slightly lower quality – the difference is small. Larry's notes suggest he thinks the entire range of 3-9 is fine.[^17] The reason for the lower quality in smaller teams is not apparent. Maybe a lack of stability? A lack of diversity of thought and experience? Reduced cross-functionality? We can't know, but it bears consideration.
182	
183	WAIT! Before you read on, remember that the whole point of this article is to stress that your mileage may vary! Don't substitute the opinions or evidence of others for your own knowledge of, and experimentation with, your teams. Start with this information, then tweak to find what works best for your team.
184	
185	<Figure
186	  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV1B}
187	  alt="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
188	  caption="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
189	/>
190	
191	## My Experience
192	So, when clients and attendees of my [training](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/) ask me what size Scrum teams should be, I don't have a "correct" answer. But I share the above data and my personal opinions and suggestions based on years of experience. Most of it is rooted in simple logic and common sense. For example, larger teams spend longer in forming, longer in normalizing, and therefore longer to reach high performance. Why? Because there are more relationships to be negotiated. As we saw before, on a team of 5, there are 10 relationships that need to form, a team of 7 has 21 relationships, and so on. More relationships take more time to build and establish trust, so that has to be factored into the decision of team size.
193	
194	Assuming everything else is equal (e.g. skills required to get the job done, diversity of thought, etc.), existing evidence supports the idea that teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They take less time to form and are as productive as larger teams. In addition, teams of 5-6 can typically cross-skill enough to cover the loss of a team member after they win the lottery.
195	
196	Personally, I would only choose a team of 7 if other pressures, like a required breadth of skills, forced it to happen. I no longer recommend teams of 8, because the additional overhead overwhelms the value of the extra person.
197	
198	With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into 2 teams. My own experience mirrors that of other Scrum trainers and coaches – separate teams of 4 and 5 get more done than their original large team.
199	
200	Why not 3 or fewer? Because it would result in too little diversity of thought, and would likely be very challenging to find 3 individuals with sufficient skills to get the job done on a complex project. There also will be very little collaboration, which correlates with the reduction in quality that Figure #2 shows (data from "Impact of Agile Quantified"). And don't forget the obvious 2-on1 power issues that may make the journey more challenging for one team member.
201	
202	All of the focus has been on the number of people in the team, but the more important question should be this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly "done" (i.e. shippable) at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, then you will want to re-examine and reconfigure to achieve a more effective team size.
203	
204	What has been your experience with team size? Too small? Too big? Just right?
205	
206	### Check out the 5 Steps to High-Performance Teams
207	As we've learned, big teams don't mean more work gets done faster. High-Performance Teams though… that's where the magic happens. Check out our [5 Steps to High-Performance Teams](/ebooks/) and get your own copy of the e-book by subscribing to our newsletter, and see what changes could help your team improve.
208	
209	Thanks to: [Peter Stevens and his own digging](https://saat-network.ch/2014/12/how-many-people-do-you-need-in-your-team/), Larry Maccherone and access to all of his work, Joseph Pelrine for pointing me to original research papers, Brent Barton for telling me about Putnam and Myers, Manoj Vadakkan and Angela Johnson for other references, and Pawel Brodzinksi, who offers [an alternate view](https://brodzinski.com/2014/01/ideal-team-size-fallacy.html).

216	</LinkList>
217	
218	<CalloutBox heading="Frequently Asked Questions About Scrum Team Size">
219	### What is the ideal Scrum team size?
220	The optimal Scrum team size is 4-6 members, based on research and practical experience. This range balances productivity, communication overhead, and team dynamics while maintaining cross-functional capabilities.

---
title: "What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size?"
date: "2020-03-13"
lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
categories:
  - 'team-dynamics-and-people'
coverImage: "@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v2-A.jpg"
excerpt: 'Discover the optimal Scrum team size based on research and 20+ years experience. Learn why 4-6 members works best, plus factors affecting team performance.'
---
import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV2A from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v2-A.jpg';
import TeamSize from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/team-size.jpg';
import ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage1 from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Parallelizable-vs-Serial-Work-image-1.jpg';
import ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage3Equation from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Parallelizable-vs-Serial-Work-image-3-equation.jpg';
import ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage2 from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Parallelizable-vs-Serial-Work-image-2.jpg';
import AmdahlsLawGraph from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Amdahls-Law-graph.jpg';
import SociometryGroupSize from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Sociometry-group-size.jpg';
import PutnamMyersStudyPersonMonths from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Putnam-Myers-study-person-months.jpg';
import LarryMaccheroneTeamSizeToPerformance from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/Larry-Maccherone-team-size-to-performance.png';
import APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV1B from '@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v1-B.jpg';

Nearly every client I work with asks me this question: 'What's the optimal Scrum team size?' The [Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#team-dev) offers very limited guidance, suggesting 3-9 people per team (exclusive of ScrumMaster and Product Owner), without giving reasons or context for those numbers. The research and 20+ years of experience reveal a more nuanced answer that could dramatically impact your team's productivity.

In many cases this question comes up as a side effect of [Sprint Planning from Hell](/blog/sprint-planning-from-hell/) or [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/) that goes on too long.

There isn't one universally correct answer for optimal team size, but there are a number of factors and trade-offs worth considering when figuring out what will work best for your team.

In this post, we'll explore the research, and I'll share my personal experiences about effective team size. While this is primarily about Scrum, the lessons are applicable for any work that is collaborative and knowledge-based.

<Figure
  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV2A}
  alt="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
  caption="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
/>

<CalloutBox heading="Key Takeaways: Optimal Scrum Team Size">
- **Best size**: There is no best size. However teams of 4-6 or often a good choice
- **Communication cost**: Relationships grow exponentially (N(N-1)/2 formula)
- **Avoid**: Teams of 8+ show diminishing returns
- **Critical factors**: Skills, stability of membership, and psychological safety matter as much as size
- **Evidence**: Multiple studies support smaller teams for knowledge work
</CalloutBox>

## Effective Scrum Team Size is More than Just a Number
When you're trying to determine what will work best, your  Team's needs should be more important than any arbitrary number. Factors you should consider include:

- A [sufficiently broad set of skills](/blog/how-to-cross-skill-and-grow-t-shaped-team-members/) to build their product – aka Cross-Functional
- Team members dedicated to one, and only one, team
- [Stable membership](/blog/stable-teams-really-do-matter/) – i.e. team membership that is consistent over a long period of time[^1]
- Diversity of thought – a sufficiently broad set of beliefs, attitudes and thinking patterns[^2]

Once the Team is formed, these are often just as important as team size when predicting success:

- Psychological safety – the environment is safe for all team members to share their ideas[^3][^4]
- Collective Intelligence of the Team – strongly correlated with average sensitivity of team members[^4]
- Equal Communication – the most expressive team member is no more than twice as expressive as the quietest[^5]
- Open-Mindedness and Willingness to Learn[^6]
- A Shared Vision of which all Team members are committed to achieving[^8]
- Clear Roles and Responsibilities[^9]
- Dynamically Shared Leadership[^10]
- External Coach – in Scrum this is the ScrumMaster

These factors don't exist in a void, so let's explore the evidence that supports what others, including myself, have discovered about team size, to help you consider what's most important for your Team. After all, there is no universal answer, there is only a range that will likely work best for your needs.

## The Problem with Arbitrary Numbers for Optimal Team Size
The earliest Scrum and XP books all suggest a team size number of 7+/-2, applying Miller's number,[^11] believed to be the number of integers you can hold in short-term memory. I'm troubled by this, since I can't see why one's ability to keep track of numbers should be correlated with team size. In addition, more recent research[^12] has shown that, as the things you're keeping track of become more complex, the number of items you can keep in your short-term memory drops to 4 or less. Clearly, we need more useful sources.

Many other coaches cite historical examples going back to the Roman army, which used small military unit sizes of around 8 people. Others observe bonobos, one of the closest genetic relatives to humans, often split into groups of 6-7 to forage for a day. Both of these conveniently support the 7+/-2 number, but since neither example is about teams doing knowledge work, the relevance of these for Scrum is limited.

## What Happens to Relationships When Teams Get Large?
<Figure
  src={TeamSize}
  alt="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
  caption="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
/>

In a team, each individual will connect with another individual and form a unique relationship. The bigger the team, the more the relationships. The equation that describes this is N (N – 1)/2. But what exactly does that _mean_? More importantly, how is it supposed to help you? Let's start by treating it as a high-school math problem, then turn it into something we can actually use in real life.

The above equation tells us how many different relationships will exist within a team of a certain size. N = the number of people in the team. So, in the first example of a team of 5 people, for N=5 you have 10 relationships: 10 different combinations of team members relating with other team members.

In the second example, n=7, you have 21 relationships, and at n=9 in the third image you have 36 relationships.  Each pair of people represents one relationship, and that relationship is how they collaborate. High-performing teams, by their nature, must have strong relationships between each of the team members to collaborative effectively.

Why does this matter, and how can it help you? Each new person adds some individual productivity to the Team, but they also increase the communications overhead in the form of an exponentially growing number of relationships. To increase a team from 5 to 7 people, you have to more than double the number of relationships. To go from 7 to 9, you don't quite double it, but the jump is still large.

Just how expensive is it to maintain these relationships? Anecdotally, having studied team member interactions at clients' sites, I can say that in teams of 7-8 people, upwards of 90 minutes per person each day is spent interacting with other team members.[^13] This excludes pair programming time. Some of the interaction is talking about work, but just as much is spent socializing. This is good and important because it's the combination of work and socializing that builds a team's resilience and ability to handle challenges effectively (see the water cooler section in "[Five Steps Towards Creating High-Performance Teams](/learn/)").

So the number of relationships between team members, and the time investment they require, needs to be a factor considered when choosing team size because it will influence productivity.

A general rule of thumb suggests that people typically have from 3½ to 5 hours of productive time at work each day. As a team gets larger, we either lose productivity or, more often, we start to withdraw socially rather than sacrifice productive time for interacting with our peers because the communication costs for each team member is becoming too high to afford. We need strong relationships to become a high-performing team but, as group size grows, we start to avoid the interactions that build those relationships.[^14]

### Many Hands Make Light Work… But Only to a Point
We all want to believe that if we go from 1 person to 2 people, or from 2 to 4 people, we will get a doubling of the amount of work done. Yet, we know intuitively that isn't the case.

What we're missing is _why_. Enter "[Amdahl's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)." The formula, first presented in 1967, estimates how much of a speedup might be gained if we took a computing task and ran parts of it in parallel. If that sounds like gobbledygook, it just means sometimes programs have parts that can be worked on by multiple processors at the same time (i.e. parallel processing), but other parts that must be done one at a time (i.e. serial programming).

<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage1}
  alt="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>

The first picture imagines work done by one processor. It takes 5 units of time.

If we take the 5 units of work and apply 3 processors to the parts that can be done concurrently (parallel), it doesn't take 1 and 2/3 units of time (5 divided by 3) to complete. Instead, it takes 3 units because 2 of the units of work can only be done by one processor (serial). It's certainly an improvement in time, but not as much as you might expect.

The math to explain the problem might look intimidating at first:

<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage3Equation}
  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>


<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage2}
  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>

Work in teams has similar properties. In fact, if we turn it into a graph, we see just how inefficient increased team size can be:

<Figure
  src={AmdahlsLawGraph}
  alt="Amdahl's Law graph."
  caption="Amdahl's Law graph."
/>

Just focus for now on the 80% line (teal, at the top) of the graph. Let's be optimistic (and unrealistic) and assume that 80% of the work can be done by working in parallel. This suggests that the more people doing it, the faster it will get done – right?  Ah, but wait. If we go from 1 person to 2 people, we don't get twice as much done. To get a 2 times improvement in work completed, we actually need 3 people. 7 people only create a 3.2 times improvement over 1 person. To get 4 times as much work done as 1 person, we would need 16 people!

What happens if even less of the work can be done concurrently (parallel)? What if 50% of the work must be done in serial (red line on the graph)? Then with 9 people, we still have only a 1.8 times speedup.

What's the solution? There's no easy fix, but there are things you can do to mitigate the effect of Amdahl's Law:

- Make it so as much of the work as possible can be done in parallel. This may mean increasing cross-skilling and collaboration.
- Reduce cross-team dependencies, so there are no bottlenecks and delays.
- Increase the speed of the work process overall by improving quality and practices.

Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from [building a high-performance team](/learn/) that is an optimal size for effectiveness, communication, and quality.

## Research-Backed Evidence on Team Size
The American Sociological Association published a study by Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ on the "Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions."[^15]

<Figure
  src={SociometryGroupSize}
  alt="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
  caption="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
/>

In this study, they had participants complete a number of tasks – a mix of Production (writing), Discussion, and Problem-Solving. The participants were placed in different groups sized from 2 to 7. After completing each task, volunteers were asked a number of questions, including two that this graph displays: "was your group too small?", "was your group too large?". As you can see from the graph, groups around 4-5 in size seemed to have the least negative reaction. The oft-cited number is 4.6. The participants were undergraduate students (all men, sadly), the tasks had a cognitive load but were not programming, and the groups weren't together long enough for a real sense of a "team" to form. Nonetheless, it is an interesting data point.

By the time Hackman wrote the book _Leading Teams_, his rule of thumb for team size was 6.

Jennifer Mueller cited in "[Is Your Team Too Big? Too Small? What's the Right Number?](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/is-your-team-too-big-too-small-whats-the-right-number-2/):"

> _if companies are dealing with coordination tasks and motivational issues, and you ask, 'What is your team size and what is optimal?' that correlates to a team of six. "Above and beyond five, and you begin to see diminishing motivation," says Mueller. "After the fifth person, you look for cliques. And the number of people who speak at any one time? That's harder to manage in a group of five or more."_

It's not just personal opinions from team members that teach us about optimal group size: we also have objective statistics. Putnam and Myers surveyed data from 491 software projects in a large corporation.[^16] These were projects with 35,000 – 90,000 source lines of code. They broke projects down into buckets based on the number of people involved in the project: 1.5-3, 3-5, 5-7, 9-11, and 15-20. On average, the smaller groups (3-5, 5-7) took significantly less time (11.9 and 11.6 months, respectively) than the larger groups (17.1 and 16.29 months) to complete similar-sized projects.

When you multiply the number of team members times the number of months, you get a graph that is even more shocking:

<Figure
  src={PutnamMyersStudyPersonMonths}
  alt="Putnam Myers study graph. "
  caption="Putnam Myers study graph. "
/>

A team of 9-11 people took  around2.5-3.5 times as long as teams of 5-7 and 3-5 to complete projects of a similar size. That suggests that teams larger than seven in this dataset were just a way to spend money faster because of the increased team size but reduced net performance.

## Evidence from Agile Projects
Larry Maccherone, in his work through both Rally, Tasktop, and AgileCraft, has helped build large datasets about practices in Agile Teams. His data shows:

<Figure
  src={LarryMaccheroneTeamSizeToPerformance}
  alt="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
  caption="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
/>

Based on Larry's data, it would appear that teams of 1-3 are more productive but have lower quality. Teams of 3-5 are marginally more productive than 5-9, although they might still have slightly lower quality – the difference is small. Larry's notes suggest he thinks the entire range of 3-9 is fine.[^17] The reason for the lower quality in smaller teams is not apparent. Maybe a lack of stability? A lack of diversity of thought and experience? Reduced cross-functionality? We can't know, but it bears consideration.

WAIT! Before you read on, remember that the whole point of this article is to stress that your mileage may vary! Don't substitute the opinions or evidence of others for your own knowledge of, and experimentation with, your teams. Start with this information, then tweak to find what works best for your team.

<Figure
  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV1B}
  alt="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
  caption="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
/>

## My Experience
So, when clients and attendees of my [training](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/) ask me what size Scrum teams should be, I don't have a "correct" answer. But I share the above data and my personal opinions and suggestions based on years of experience. Most of it is rooted in simple logic and common sense. For example, larger teams spend longer in forming, longer in normalizing, and therefore longer to reach high performance. Why? Because there are more relationships to be negotiated. As we saw before, on a team of 5, there are 10 relationships that need to form, a team of 7 has 21 relationships, and so on. More relationships take more time to build and establish trust, so that has to be factored into the decision of team size.

Assuming everything else is equal (e.g. skills required to get the job done, diversity of thought, etc.), existing evidence supports the idea that teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They take less time to form and are as productive as larger teams. In addition, teams of 5-6 can typically cross-skill enough to cover the loss of a team member after they win the lottery.

Personally, I would only choose a team of 7 if other pressures, like a required breadth of skills, forced it to happen. I no longer recommend teams of 8, because the additional overhead overwhelms the value of the extra person.

With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into 2 teams. My own experience mirrors that of other Scrum trainers and coaches – separate teams of 4 and 5 get more done than their original large team.

Why not 3 or fewer? Because it would result in too little diversity of thought, and would likely be very challenging to find 3 individuals with sufficient skills to get the job done on a complex project. There also will be very little collaboration, which correlates with the reduction in quality that Figure #2 shows (data from "Impact of Agile Quantified"). And don't forget the obvious 2-on1 power issues that may make the journey more challenging for one team member.

All of the focus has been on the number of people in the team, but the more important question should be this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly "done" (i.e. shippable) at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, then you will want to re-examine and reconfigure to achieve a more effective team size.

What has been your experience with team size? Too small? Too big? Just right?

### Check out the 5 Steps to High-Performance Teams
As we've learned, big teams don't mean more work gets done faster. High-Performance Teams though… that's where the magic happens. Check out our [5 Steps to High-Performance Teams](/ebooks/) and get your own copy of the e-book by subscribing to our newsletter, and see what changes could help your team improve.

Thanks to: [Peter Stevens and his own digging](https://saat-network.ch/2014/12/how-many-people-do-you-need-in-your-team/), Larry Maccherone and access to all of his work, Joseph Pelrine for pointing me to original research papers, Brent Barton for telling me about Putnam and Myers, Manoj Vadakkan and Angela Johnson for other references, and Pawel Brodzinksi, who offers [an alternate view](https://brodzinski.com/2014/01/ideal-team-size-fallacy.html).

<LinkList heading = "Related Blog Entries">
    - [Collaboration, Over Work in Isolation](/blog/collaboration-over-work-in-isolation/)
    - [Characteristics of Effective Scrum Teams](/blog/characteristics-of-effective-scrum-teams/)
    - [How to Build a Powerful Team from Scratch](/blog/how-to-build-a-powerful-team-from-scratch/)
    - [The Spotify Model: Why Copying It Doesn't Work](/blog/the-spotify-model-of-scaling-spotify-doesnt-use-it-neither-should-you/)
</LinkList>

<CalloutBox heading="Frequently Asked Questions About Scrum Team Size">
### What is the ideal Scrum team size?
The optimal Scrum team size is 4-6 members, based on research and practical experience. This range balances productivity, communication overhead, and team dynamics while maintaining cross-functional capabilities.

### Why does the Scrum Guide recommend 3-9 people?
The Scrum Guide doesn't provide a clear reason. Neither Jeff or Ken are known for providing explanations of the Scrum Guide.

### What happens if my Scrum team is too large?
Teams larger than 7 experience exponentially growing communication overhead, reduced productivity per person, longer time to form high-performing relationships, and decreased individual contribution.

### Can a Scrum team have 2-3 people?
While possible, teams of 2-3 lack diversity of thought, struggle with skill coverage, and show reduced quality in Agile metrics. Teams of 4+ perform better overall.
</CalloutBox>

[^5]: Anita Williams Woolley, Christopher F. Chabris, Alex Pentland, Nada Hashmi, Thomas W. Malone. Evidence for a Collective Intelligence Factor in the Performance of Human Groups. Science 29 Oct 2010: Vol. 330, Issue 6004, pp. 686-688
[^6]: ["The New Science of Building Great Teams" - Alex "Sandy" Pentland and also "Evidence for a Collective Intelligence Factor in the Performance of Human Groups"](https://hbr.org/2012/04/the-new-science-of-building-great-teams)
[^7]: [The Wisdom of Teams: Creating the High-Performance Organization by Jon Katzenbach and Douglas Smith – stated that the Skills Potential are as important as the skills people currently have in predicting effectiveness.](https://www.amazon.ca/Wisdom-Teams-Creating-High-Performance-Organization/dp/1633691063/&tag=notesfromatoo-2)

Nearly every client I work with asks me this question: 'What's the optimal Scrum team size?' The [Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#team-dev) offers very limited guidance, suggesting {~~3-9 people per team (exclusive of ScrumMaster and Product Owner)~>a Scrum Team of typically 10 or fewer people~~}{>>Claude: 2020 Scrum Guide update -- it dropped the old "3-9 Developers, exclusive of SM and PO" and now says the Scrum Team is "typically 10 or fewer people," counting the one ScrumMaster and one Product Owner in that number. Your 4-6 recommendation is unaffected.<<}, without giving reasons or context for those numbers. The research and 20+ years of experience reveal a more nuanced answer that could dramatically impact your team's productivity.

In many cases this question comes up as a side effect of [Sprint Planning from Hell](/blog/sprint-planning-from-hell/) or [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/) that goes on too long.

There isn't one universally correct answer for optimal team size, but there are a number of factors and trade-offs worth considering when figuring out what will work best for your team.

In this post, we'll explore the research, and I'll share my personal experiences about effective team size. While this is primarily about Scrum, the lessons are applicable for any work that is collaborative and knowledge-based.

<Figure
  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV2A}
  alt="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
  caption="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
/>

<CalloutBox heading="Key Takeaways: Optimal Scrum Team Size">
- **Best size**: There is no best size. However teams of 4-6 or often a good choice
- **Communication cost**: Relationships grow exponentially (N(N-1)/2 formula)
- **Avoid**: Teams of 8+ show diminishing returns
- **Critical factors**: Skills, stability of membership, and psychological safety matter as much as size
- **Evidence**: Multiple studies support smaller teams for knowledge work
</CalloutBox>

## Effective Scrum Team Size is More than Just a Number
When you're trying to determine what will work best, your  Team's needs should be more important than any arbitrary number. Factors you should consider include:

- A [sufficiently broad set of skills](/blog/how-to-cross-skill-and-grow-t-shaped-team-members/) to build their product – aka Cross-Functional
- Team members dedicated to one, and only one, team
- [Stable membership](/blog/stable-teams-really-do-matter/) – i.e. team membership that is consistent over a long period of time[^1]
- Diversity of thought – a sufficiently broad set of beliefs, attitudes and thinking patterns[^2]

Once the Team is formed, these are often just as important as team size when predicting success:

- Psychological safety – the environment is safe for all team members to share their ideas[^3][^4]
- Collective Intelligence of the Team – strongly correlated with average sensitivity of team members[^4]
- Equal Communication – the most expressive team member is no more than twice as expressive as the quietest[^5]
- Open-Mindedness and Willingness to Learn[^6]
- A Shared Vision of which all Team members are committed to achieving[^8]
- Clear Roles and Responsibilities[^9]
- Dynamically Shared Leadership[^10]
- External Coach – in Scrum this is the ScrumMaster

These factors don't exist in a void, so let's explore the evidence that supports what others, including myself, have discovered about team size, to help you consider what's most important for your Team. After all, there is no universal answer, there is only a range that will likely work best for your needs.

## The Problem with Arbitrary Numbers for Optimal Team Size
The earliest Scrum and XP books all suggest a team size number of 7+/-2, applying Miller's number,[^11] believed to be the number of integers you can hold in short-term memory. I'm troubled by this, since I can't see why one's ability to keep track of numbers should be correlated with team size. In addition, more recent research[^12] has shown that, as the things you're keeping track of become more complex, the number of items you can keep in your short-term memory drops to 4 or less. Clearly, we need more useful sources.

Many other coaches cite historical examples going back to the Roman army, which used small military unit sizes of around 8 people. Others observe bonobos, one of the closest genetic relatives to humans, often split into groups of 6-7 to forage for a day. Both of these conveniently support the 7+/-2 number, but since neither example is about teams doing knowledge work, the relevance of these for Scrum is limited.

## What Happens to Relationships When Teams Get Large?
<Figure
  src={TeamSize}
  alt="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
  caption="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
/>

In a team, each individual will connect with another individual and form a unique relationship. The bigger the team, the more the relationships. The equation that describes this is N (N – 1)/2. But what exactly does that _mean_? More importantly, how is it supposed to help you? Let's start by treating it as a high-school math problem, then turn it into something we can actually use in real life.

The above equation tells us how many different relationships will exist within a team of a certain size. N = the number of people in the team. So, in the first example of a team of 5 people, for N=5 you have 10 relationships: 10 different combinations of team members relating with other team members.

In the second example, n=7, you have 21 relationships, and at n=9 in the third image you have 36 relationships.  Each pair of people represents one relationship, and that relationship is how they collaborate. High-performing teams, by their nature, must have strong relationships between each of the team members to collaborative effectively.

Why does this matter, and how can it help you? Each new person adds some individual productivity to the Team, but they also increase the communications overhead in the form of an exponentially growing number of relationships. To increase a team from 5 to 7 people, you have to more than double the number of relationships. To go from 7 to 9, you don't quite double it, but the jump is still large.

Just how expensive is it to maintain these relationships? Anecdotally, having studied team member interactions at clients' sites, I can say that in teams of 7-8 people, upwards of 90 minutes per person each day is spent interacting with other team members.[^13] This excludes pair programming time. Some of the interaction is talking about work, but just as much is spent socializing. This is good and important because it's the combination of work and socializing that builds a team's resilience and ability to handle challenges effectively (see the water cooler section in "[Five Steps Towards Creating High-Performance Teams](/learn/)").

So the number of relationships between team members, and the time investment they require, needs to be a factor considered when choosing team size because it will influence productivity.

A general rule of thumb suggests that people typically have from 3½ to 5 hours of productive time at work each day. As a team gets larger, we either lose productivity or, more often, we start to withdraw socially rather than sacrifice productive time for interacting with our peers because the communication costs for each team member is becoming too high to afford. We need strong relationships to become a high-performing team but, as group size grows, we start to avoid the interactions that build those relationships.[^14]

### Many Hands Make Light Work… But Only to a Point
We all want to believe that if we go from 1 person to 2 people, or from 2 to 4 people, we will get a doubling of the amount of work done. Yet, we know intuitively that isn't the case.

What we're missing is _why_. Enter "[Amdahl's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)." The formula, first presented in 1967, estimates how much of a speedup might be gained if we took a computing task and ran parts of it in parallel. If that sounds like gobbledygook, it just means sometimes programs have parts that can be worked on by multiple processors at the same time (i.e. parallel processing), but other parts that must be done one at a time (i.e. serial programming).

<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage1}
  alt="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>

The first picture imagines work done by one processor. It takes 5 units of time.

If we take the 5 units of work and apply 3 processors to the parts that can be done concurrently (parallel), it doesn't take 1 and 2/3 units of time (5 divided by 3) to complete. Instead, it takes 3 units because 2 of the units of work can only be done by one processor (serial). It's certainly an improvement in time, but not as much as you might expect.

The math to explain the problem might look intimidating at first:

<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage3Equation}
  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>


<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage2}
  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>

Work in teams has similar properties. In fact, if we turn it into a graph, we see just how inefficient increased team size can be:

<Figure
  src={AmdahlsLawGraph}
  alt="Amdahl's Law graph."
  caption="Amdahl's Law graph."
/>

Just focus for now on the 80% line (teal, at the top) of the graph. Let's be optimistic (and unrealistic) and assume that 80% of the work can be done by working in parallel. This suggests that the more people doing it, the faster it will get done – right?  Ah, but wait. If we go from 1 person to 2 people, we don't get twice as much done. To get a 2 times improvement in work completed, we actually need 3 people. 7 people only create a 3.2 times improvement over 1 person. To get 4 times as much work done as 1 person, we would need 16 people!

What happens if even less of the work can be done concurrently (parallel)? What if 50% of the work must be done in serial (red line on the graph)? Then with 9 people, we still have only a 1.8 times speedup.

What's the solution? There's no easy fix, but there are things you can do to mitigate the effect of Amdahl's Law:

- Make it so as much of the work as possible can be done in parallel. This may mean increasing cross-skilling and collaboration.
- Reduce cross-team dependencies, so there are no bottlenecks and delays.
- Increase the speed of the work process overall by improving quality and practices.

Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from [building a high-performance team](/learn/) that is an optimal size for effectiveness, communication, and quality.

## Research-Backed Evidence on Team Size
The American Sociological Association published a study by Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ on the "Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions."[^15]

<Figure
  src={SociometryGroupSize}
  alt="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
  caption="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
/>

In this study, they had participants complete a number of tasks – a mix of Production (writing), Discussion, and Problem-Solving. The participants were placed in different groups sized from 2 to 7. After completing each task, volunteers were asked a number of questions, including two that this graph displays: "was your group too small?", "was your group too large?". As you can see from the graph, groups around 4-5 in size seemed to have the least negative reaction. The oft-cited number is 4.6. The participants were undergraduate students (all men, sadly), the tasks had a cognitive load but were not programming, and the groups weren't together long enough for a real sense of a "team" to form. Nonetheless, it is an interesting data point.

By the time Hackman wrote the book _Leading Teams_, his rule of thumb for team size was 6.

Jennifer Mueller cited in "[Is Your Team Too Big? Too Small? What's the Right Number?](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/is-your-team-too-big-too-small-whats-the-right-number-2/):"

> _if companies are dealing with coordination tasks and motivational issues, and you ask, 'What is your team size and what is optimal?' that correlates to a team of six. "Above and beyond five, and you begin to see diminishing motivation," says Mueller. "After the fifth person, you look for cliques. And the number of people who speak at any one time? That's harder to manage in a group of five or more."_

It's not just personal opinions from team members that teach us about optimal group size: we also have objective statistics. Putnam and Myers surveyed data from 491 software projects in a large corporation.[^16] These were projects with 35,000 – 90,000 source lines of code. They broke projects down into buckets based on the number of people involved in the project: 1.5-3, 3-5, 5-7, 9-11, and 15-20. On average, the smaller groups (3-5, 5-7) took significantly less time (11.9 and 11.6 months, respectively) than the larger groups (17.1 and 16.29 months) to complete similar-sized projects.

When you multiply the number of team members times the number of months, you get a graph that is even more shocking:

<Figure
  src={PutnamMyersStudyPersonMonths}
  alt="Putnam Myers study graph. "
  caption="Putnam Myers study graph. "
/>

A team of 9-11 people took  around2.5-3.5 times as long as teams of 5-7 and 3-5 to complete projects of a similar size. That suggests that teams larger than seven in this dataset were just a way to spend money faster because of the increased team size but reduced net performance.

## Evidence from Agile Projects
Larry Maccherone, in his work through both Rally, Tasktop, and AgileCraft, has helped build large datasets about practices in Agile Teams. His data shows:

<Figure
  src={LarryMaccheroneTeamSizeToPerformance}
  alt="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
  caption="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
/>

Based on Larry's data, it would appear that teams of 1-3 are more productive but have lower quality. Teams of 3-5 are marginally more productive than 5-9, although they might still have slightly lower quality – the difference is small. Larry's notes suggest he thinks the entire range of 3-9 is fine.[^17] The reason for the lower quality in smaller teams is not apparent. Maybe a lack of stability? A lack of diversity of thought and experience? Reduced cross-functionality? We can't know, but it bears consideration.

WAIT! Before you read on, remember that the whole point of this article is to stress that your mileage may vary! Don't substitute the opinions or evidence of others for your own knowledge of, and experimentation with, your teams. Start with this information, then tweak to find what works best for your team.

<Figure
  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV1B}
  alt="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
  caption="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
/>

## My Experience
So, when clients and attendees of my [training](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/) ask me what size Scrum teams should be, I don't have a "correct" answer. But I share the above data and my personal opinions and suggestions based on years of experience. Most of it is rooted in simple logic and common sense. For example, larger teams spend longer in forming, longer in normalizing, and therefore longer to reach high performance. Why? Because there are more relationships to be negotiated. As we saw before, on a team of 5, there are 10 relationships that need to form, a team of 7 has 21 relationships, and so on. More relationships take more time to build and establish trust, so that has to be factored into the decision of team size.

Assuming everything else is equal (e.g. skills required to get the job done, diversity of thought, etc.), existing evidence supports the idea that teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They take less time to form and are as productive as larger teams. In addition, teams of 5-6 can typically cross-skill enough to cover the loss of a team member after they win the lottery.

Personally, I would only choose a team of 7 if other pressures, like a required breadth of skills, forced it to happen. I no longer recommend teams of 8, because the additional overhead overwhelms the value of the extra person.

With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into 2 teams. My own experience mirrors that of other Scrum trainers and coaches – separate teams of 4 and 5 get more done than their original large team.

Why not 3 or fewer? Because it would result in too little diversity of thought, and would likely be very challenging to find 3 individuals with sufficient skills to get the job done on a complex project. There also will be very little collaboration, which correlates with the reduction in quality that Figure #2 shows (data from "Impact of Agile Quantified"). And don't forget the obvious 2-on1 power issues that may make the journey more challenging for one team member.

All of the focus has been on the number of people in the team, but the more important question should be this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly "done" (i.e. shippable) at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, then you will want to re-examine and reconfigure to achieve a more effective team size.

What has been your experience with team size? Too small? Too big? Just right?

### Check out the 5 Steps to High-Performance Teams
As we've learned, big teams don't mean more work gets done faster. High-Performance Teams though… that's where the magic happens. Check out our [5 Steps to High-Performance Teams](/ebooks/) and get your own copy of the e-book by subscribing to our newsletter, and see what changes could help your team improve.

Thanks to: [Peter Stevens and his own digging](https://saat-network.ch/2014/12/how-many-people-do-you-need-in-your-team/), Larry Maccherone and access to all of his work, Joseph Pelrine for pointing me to original research papers, Brent Barton for telling me about Putnam and Myers, Manoj Vadakkan and Angela Johnson for other references, and Pawel Brodzinksi, who offers [an alternate view](https://brodzinski.com/2014/01/ideal-team-size-fallacy.html).

    - [Collaboration, Over Work in Isolation](/blog/collaboration-over-work-in-isolation/)
    - [Characteristics of Effective Scrum Teams](/blog/characteristics-of-effective-scrum-teams/)
    - [How to Build a Powerful Team from Scratch](/blog/how-to-build-a-powerful-team-from-scratch/)
    - [The Spotify Model: Why Copying It Doesn't Work](/blog/the-spotify-model-of-scaling-spotify-doesnt-use-it-neither-should-you/)
</LinkList>

<CalloutBox heading="Frequently Asked Questions About Scrum Team Size">
### What is the ideal Scrum team size?
The optimal Scrum team size is 4-6 members, based on research and practical experience. This range balances productivity, communication overhead, and team dynamics while maintaining cross-functional capabilities.

### Why does the Scrum Guide {~~recommend 3-9 people~>suggest 10 or fewer people~~}?{>>Claude: same 2020 update -- "10 or fewer" replaced the old "3-9." The "no clear reason" answer below still holds.<<}
The Scrum Guide doesn't provide a clear reason. Neither Jeff or Ken are known for providing explanations of the Scrum Guide.

### What happens if my Scrum team is too large?
Teams larger than 7 experience exponentially growing communication overhead, reduced productivity per person, longer time to form high-performing relationships, and decreased individual contribution.

### Can a Scrum team have 2-3 people?
While possible, teams of 2-3 lack diversity of thought, struggle with skill coverage, and show reduced quality in Agile metrics. Teams of 4+ perform better overall.
</CalloutBox>

## The Problem with Arbitrary Numbers for Optimal Team Size
The earliest Scrum and XP books all suggest a team size number of 7+/-2, applying Miller's number,[^11] believed to be the number of integers you can hold in short-term memory. I'm troubled by this, since I can't see why one's ability to keep track of numbers should be correlated with team size. In addition, more recent research[^12] has shown that, as the things you're keeping track of become more complex, the number of items you can keep in your short-term memory drops to 4 or less. Clearly, we need more useful sources.

Many other coaches cite historical examples going back to the Roman army, which used small military unit sizes of around 8 people. Others observe bonobos, one of the closest genetic relatives to humans, often split into groups of 6-7 to forage for a day. Both of these conveniently support the 7+/-2 number, but since neither example is about teams doing knowledge work, the relevance of these for Scrum is limited.

## What Happens to Relationships When Teams Get Large?
<Figure
  src={TeamSize}
  alt="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
  caption="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
/>

In a team, each individual will connect with another individual and form a unique relationship. The bigger the team, the more the relationships. The equation that describes this is N (N – 1)/2. But what exactly does that _mean_? More importantly, how is it supposed to help you? Let's start by treating it as a high-school math problem, then turn it into something we can actually use in real life.

The above equation tells us how many different relationships will exist within a team of a certain size. N = the number of people in the team. So, in the first example of a team of 5 people, for N=5 you have 10 relationships: 10 different combinations of team members relating with other team members.

In the second example, n=7, you have 21 relationships, and at n=9 in the third image you have 36 relationships.  Each pair of people represents one relationship, and that relationship is how they collaborate. High-performing teams, by their nature, must have strong relationships between each of the team members to collaborative effectively.

Why does this matter, and how can it help you? Each new person adds some individual productivity to the Team, but they also increase the communications overhead in the form of an exponentially growing number of relationships. To increase a team from 5 to 7 people, you have to more than double the number of relationships. To go from 7 to 9, you don't quite double it, but the jump is still large.

Just how expensive is it to maintain these relationships? Anecdotally, having studied team member interactions at clients' sites, I can say that in teams of 7-8 people, upwards of 90 minutes per person each day is spent interacting with other team members.[^13] This excludes pair programming time. Some of the interaction is talking about work, but just as much is spent socializing. This is good and important because it's the combination of work and socializing that builds a team's resilience and ability to handle challenges effectively (see the water cooler section in "[Five Steps Towards Creating High-Performance Teams](/learn/)").

So the number of relationships between team members, and the time investment they require, needs to be a factor considered when choosing team size because it will influence productivity.

A general rule of thumb suggests that people typically have from 3½ to 5 hours of productive time at work each day. As a team gets larger, we either lose productivity or, more often, we start to withdraw socially rather than sacrifice productive time for interacting with our peers because the communication costs for each team member is becoming too high to afford. We need strong relationships to become a high-performing team but, as group size grows, we start to avoid the interactions that build those relationships.[^14]

### Many Hands Make Light Work… But Only to a Point
We all want to believe that if we go from 1 person to 2 people, or from 2 to 4 people, we will get a doubling of the amount of work done. Yet, we know intuitively that isn't the case.

What we're missing is _why_. Enter "[Amdahl's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)." The formula, first presented in 1967, estimates how much of a speedup might be gained if we took a computing task and ran parts of it in parallel. If that sounds like gobbledygook, it just means sometimes programs have parts that can be worked on by multiple processors at the same time (i.e. parallel processing), but other parts that must be done one at a time (i.e. serial programming).

<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage1}
  alt="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Scrum Team Size - Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>

The first picture imagines work done by one processor. It takes 5 units of time.

If we take the 5 units of work and apply 3 processors to the parts that can be done concurrently (parallel), it doesn't take 1 and 2/3 units of time (5 divided by 3) to complete. Instead, it takes 3 units because 2 of the units of work can only be done by one processor (serial). It's certainly an improvement in time, but not as much as you might expect.

The math to explain the problem might look intimidating at first:

<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage3Equation}
  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>


<Figure
  src={ParallelizableVsSerialWorkImage2}
  alt="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
  caption="Parallelizable vs Serial Work."
/>

Work in teams has similar properties. In fact, if we turn it into a graph, we see just how inefficient increased team size can be:

<Figure
  src={AmdahlsLawGraph}
  alt="Amdahl's Law graph."
  caption="Amdahl's Law graph."
/>

Just focus for now on the 80% line (teal, at the top) of the graph. Let's be optimistic (and unrealistic) and assume that 80% of the work can be done by working in parallel. This suggests that the more people doing it, the faster it will get done – right?  Ah, but wait. If we go from 1 person to 2 people, we don't get twice as much done. To get a 2 times improvement in work completed, we actually need 3 people. 7 people only create a 3.2 times improvement over 1 person. To get 4 times as much work done as 1 person, we would need 16 people!

What happens if even less of the work can be done concurrently (parallel)? What if 50% of the work must be done in serial (red line on the graph)? Then with 9 people, we still have only a 1.8 times speedup.

What's the solution? There's no easy fix, but there are things you can do to mitigate the effect of Amdahl's Law:

- Make it so as much of the work as possible can be done in parallel. This may mean increasing cross-skilling and collaboration.
- Reduce cross-team dependencies, so there are no bottlenecks and delays.
- Increase the speed of the work process overall by improving quality and practices.

Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from [building a high-performance team](/learn/) that is an optimal size for effectiveness, communication, and quality.

## Research-Backed Evidence on Team Size
The American Sociological Association published a study by Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ on the "Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions."[^15]

<Figure
  src={SociometryGroupSize}
  alt="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
  caption="Source: Hackman JR, Vidmar NJ. Effects of size and task type on group performance and member reactions. Sociometry. 1970;33 :37-54."
/>

In this study, they had participants complete a number of tasks – a mix of Production (writing), Discussion, and Problem-Solving. The participants were placed in different groups sized from 2 to 7. After completing each task, volunteers were asked a number of questions, including two that this graph displays: "was your group too small?", "was your group too large?". As you can see from the graph, groups around 4-5 in size seemed to have the least negative reaction. The oft-cited number is 4.6. The participants were undergraduate students (all men, sadly), the tasks had a cognitive load but were not programming, and the groups weren't together long enough for a real sense of a "team" to form. Nonetheless, it is an interesting data point.

By the time Hackman wrote the book _Leading Teams_, his rule of thumb for team size was 6.

Jennifer Mueller cited in "[Is Your Team Too Big? Too Small? What's the Right Number?](https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/is-your-team-too-big-too-small-whats-the-right-number-2/):"

> _if companies are dealing with coordination tasks and motivational issues, and you ask, 'What is your team size and what is optimal?' that correlates to a team of six. "Above and beyond five, and you begin to see diminishing motivation," says Mueller. "After the fifth person, you look for cliques. And the number of people who speak at any one time? That's harder to manage in a group of five or more."_

It's not just personal opinions from team members that teach us about optimal group size: we also have objective statistics. Putnam and Myers surveyed data from 491 software projects in a large corporation.[^16] These were projects with 35,000 – 90,000 source lines of code. They broke projects down into buckets based on the number of people involved in the project: 1.5-3, 3-5, 5-7, 9-11, and 15-20. On average, the smaller groups (3-5, 5-7) took significantly less time (11.9 and 11.6 months, respectively) than the larger groups (17.1 and 16.29 months) to complete similar-sized projects.

When you multiply the number of team members times the number of months, you get a graph that is even more shocking:

<Figure
  src={PutnamMyersStudyPersonMonths}
  alt="Putnam Myers study graph. "
  caption="Putnam Myers study graph. "
/>

A team of 9-11 people took  around2.5-3.5 times as long as teams of 5-7 and 3-5 to complete projects of a similar size. That suggests that teams larger than seven in this dataset were just a way to spend money faster because of the increased team size but reduced net performance.

## Evidence from Agile Projects
Larry Maccherone, in his work through both Rally, Tasktop, and AgileCraft, has helped build large datasets about practices in Agile Teams. His data shows:

<Figure
  src={LarryMaccheroneTeamSizeToPerformance}
  alt="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
  caption="Used with Permission from Larry Maccherone – from Impact of Agile Quantified Late 2014."
/>

Based on Larry's data, it would appear that teams of 1-3 are more productive but have lower quality. Teams of 3-5 are marginally more productive than 5-9, although they might still have slightly lower quality – the difference is small. Larry's notes suggest he thinks the entire range of 3-9 is fine.[^17] The reason for the lower quality in smaller teams is not apparent. Maybe a lack of stability? A lack of diversity of thought and experience? Reduced cross-functionality? We can't know, but it bears consideration.

WAIT! Before you read on, remember that the whole point of this article is to stress that your mileage may vary! Don't substitute the opinions or evidence of others for your own knowledge of, and experimentation with, your teams. Start with this information, then tweak to find what works best for your team.

<Figure
  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV1B}
  alt="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
  caption="Small Scrum teams of 5-6 members have better engagement with each other."
/>

## My Experience
So, when clients and attendees of my [training](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/) ask me what size Scrum teams should be, I don't have a "correct" answer. But I share the above data and my personal opinions and suggestions based on years of experience. Most of it is rooted in simple logic and common sense. For example, larger teams spend longer in forming, longer in normalizing, and therefore longer to reach high performance. Why? Because there are more relationships to be negotiated. As we saw before, on a team of 5, there are 10 relationships that need to form, a team of 7 has 21 relationships, and so on. More relationships take more time to build and establish trust, so that has to be factored into the decision of team size.

Assuming everything else is equal (e.g. skills required to get the job done, diversity of thought, etc.), existing evidence supports the idea that teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They take less time to form and are as productive as larger teams. In addition, teams of 5-6 can typically cross-skill enough to cover the loss of a team member after they win the lottery.

Personally, I would only choose a team of 7 if other pressures, like a required breadth of skills, forced it to happen. I no longer recommend teams of 8, because the additional overhead overwhelms the value of the extra person.

With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into 2 teams. My own experience mirrors that of other Scrum trainers and coaches – separate teams of 4 and 5 get more done than their original large team.

Why not 3 or fewer? Because it would result in too little diversity of thought, and would likely be very challenging to find 3 individuals with sufficient skills to get the job done on a complex project. There also will be very little collaboration, which correlates with the reduction in quality that Figure #2 shows (data from "Impact of Agile Quantified"). And don't forget the obvious 2-on1 power issues that may make the journey more challenging for one team member.

All of the focus has been on the number of people in the team, but the more important question should be this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly "done" (i.e. shippable) at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, then you will want to re-examine and reconfigure to achieve a more effective team size.

What has been your experience with team size? Too small? Too big? Just right?

### Check out the 5 Steps to High-Performance Teams
As we've learned, big teams don't mean more work gets done faster. High-Performance Teams though… that's where the magic happens. Check out our [5 Steps to High-Performance Teams](/ebooks/) and get your own copy of the e-book by subscribing to our newsletter, and see what changes could help your team improve.
