<CalloutBox heading="Frequently Asked Questions About Scrum Team Size">
### What is the ideal Scrum team size?
The optimal Scrum team size is 4-6 members, based on research and practical experience. This range balances productivity, communication overhead, and team dynamics while maintaining cross-functional capabilities.

### Why does the Scrum Guide {~~recommend 3-9 people~>suggest 10 or fewer people~~}?{>>Claude: same 2020 update -- "10 or fewer" replaced the old "3-9." The "no clear reason" answer below still holds.<<}
The Scrum Guide doesn't provide a clear reason. Neither Jeff or Ken are known for providing explanations of the Scrum Guide.

### What happens if my Scrum team is too large?
Teams larger than 7 experience exponentially growing communication overhead, reduced productivity per person, longer time to form high-performing relationships, and decreased individual contribution.

### Can a Scrum team have 2-3 people?
While possible, teams of 2-3 lack diversity of thought, struggle with skill coverage, and show reduced quality in Agile metrics. Teams of 4+ perform better overall.
</CalloutBox>

+We all want to believe that if we go from 1 person to 2 people, or from 2 to 4 people, we will get a doubling of the amount of work done. Yet, we know intuitively that isn't the case.

+What we're missing is _why_. Enter "[Amdahl's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)." The formula, first presented in 1967, estimates how much of a speedup might be gained if we took a computing task and ran parts of it in parallel. If that sounds like gobbledygook, it just means sometimes programs have parts that can be worked on by multiple processors at the same time (i.e. parallel processing), but other parts that must be done one at a time (i.e. serial programming).

-What’s the solution? There’s no easy fix, but there are things you can do to mitigate the effect of Amdahl’s Law:
+What's the solution? There's no easy fix, but there are things you can do to mitigate the effect of Amdahl's Law:
- Make it so as much of the work as possible can be done in parallel. This may mean increasing cross-skilling and collaboration.
- Reduce cross-team dependencies, so there are no bottlenecks and delays.
- Increase the speed of the work process overall by improving quality and practices.

-Speed doesn’t come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from [building a high-performance team](/high-performance-teams) that is an optimal size for effectiveness, communication, and quality.

## My Experience

-So, when clients and attendees of my training ask me what size Scrum teams should be, I don’t have a “correct” answer. But I share the above data and my personal opinions and suggestions based on years of experience. Most of it is rooted in simple logic and common sense. For example, larger teams spend longer in forming, longer in normalizing, and therefore longer to reach high performance. Why? Because there are more relationships to be negotiated. As we saw before, on a team of 5, there are 10 relationships that need to form, a team of 7 has 21 relationships, and so on. More relationships take more time to build and establish trust, so that has to be factored into the decision of team size.

+So, when clients and attendees of my [training](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/) ask me what size Scrum teams should be, I don't have a "correct" answer. But I share the above data and my personal opinions and suggestions based on years of experience. Most of it is rooted in simple logic and common sense. For example, larger teams spend longer in forming, longer in normalizing, and therefore longer to reach high performance. Why? Because there are more relationships to be negotiated. As we saw before, on a team of 5, there are 10 relationships that need to form, a team of 7 has 21 relationships, and so on. More relationships take more time to build and establish trust, so that has to be factored into the decision of team size.

Assuming everything else is equal (e.g. skills required to get the job done, diversity of thought, etc.), existing evidence supports the idea that teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They take less time to form and are as productive as larger teams. In addition, teams of 5-6 can typically cross-skill enough to cover the loss of a team member after they win the lottery.

With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into 2 teams. My own experience mirrors that of other Scrum trainers and coaches – separate teams of 4 and 5 get more done than their original large team.

-Why not 3 or fewer? Because it would result in too little diversity of thought, and would likely be very challenging to find 3 individuals with sufficient skills to get the job done on a complex project. There also will be very little collaboration, which correlates with the reduction in quality that Figure #2 shows (data from “Impact of Agile Quantified”). And don’t forget the obvious 2-on1 power issues that may make the journey more challenging for one team member.

-All of the focus has been on the number of people in the team, but the more important question should be this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly “done” (i.e. shippable) at the end of every Sprint? 1	---
2	title: "What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size?"
3	date: "2020-03-13"
4	lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
5	categories:
6	  - 'team-dynamics-and-people'
7	coverImage: "@/content/blog/scrum-team-size/images/APR-09_Blog-Illustrations_Mar2020_ScrumTeamSize_v2-A.jpg"
8	excerpt: 'Discover the optimal Scrum team size based on research and 20+ years experience. Learn why 4-6 members works best, plus factors affecting team performance.'
9	---
10	
11	Nearly every client I work with asks me this question: 'What's the optimal Scrum team size?' The [Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#team-dev) offers very limited guidance, suggesting a Scrum Team of typically 10 or fewer people, without giving reasons or context for those numbers. The research and 20+ years of experience reveal a more nuanced answer that could dramatically impact your team's productivity.
12	
13	In many cases this question comes up as a side effect of [Sprint Planning from Hell](/blog/sprint-planning-from-hell/) or [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/) that goes on too long.
14	
15	There isn't one universally correct answer for optimal team size, but there are a number of factors and trade-offs worth considering when figuring out what will work best for your team.
16	
17	In this post, we'll explore the research, and I'll share my personal experiences about effective team size. While this is primarily about Scrum, the lessons are applicable for any work that is collaborative and knowledge-based.
18	
19	<Figure
20	  src={APR09BlogIllustrationsMar2020ScrumTeamSizeV2A}
21	  alt="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
22	  caption="What is the Recommended Scrum Team Size? This is a larger than ideal scrum team size!"
23	/>
24	
25	<CalloutBox heading="Key Takeaways: Optimal Scrum Team Size">
26	- **Best size**: There is no best size. However teams of 4-6 or often a good choice
27	- **Communication cost**: Relationships grow exponentially (N(N-1)/2 formula)
28	- **Avoid**: Teams of 8+ show diminishing returns
29	- **Critical factors**: Skills, stability of membership, and psychological safety matter as much as size
30	- **Evidence**: Multiple studies support smaller teams for knowledge work
31	</CalloutBox>
32	
33	## Effective Scrum Team Size is More than Just a Number
34	When you're trying to determine what will work best, your  Team's needs should be more important than any arbitrary number. Factors you should consider include:
35	
36	- A [sufficiently broad set of skills](/blog/how-to-cross-skill-and-grow-t-shaped-team-members/) to build their product – aka Cross-Functional
37	- Team members dedicated to one, and only one, team
38	- [Stable membership](/blog/stable-teams-really-do-matter/) – i.e. team membership that is consistent over a long period of time[^1]
39	- Diversity of thought – a sufficiently broad set of beliefs, attitudes and thinking patterns[^2]
40	
41	Once the Team is formed, these are often just as important as team size when predicting success:
42	
43	- Psychological safety – the environment is safe for all team members to share their ideas[^3][^4]
44	- Collective Intelligence of the Team – strongly correlated with average sensitivity of team members[^4]
45	- Equal Communication – the most expressive team member is no more than twice as expressive as the quietest[^5]
46	- Open-Mindedness and Willingness to Learn[^6]
47	- A Shared Vision of which all Team members are committed to achieving[^8]
48	- Clear Roles and Responsibilities[^9]
49	- Dynamically Shared Leadership[^10]
50	- External Coach – in Scrum this is the ScrumMaster
51	
52	These factors don't exist in a void, so let's explore the evidence that supports what others, including myself, have discovered about team size, to help you consider what's most important for your Team. After all, there is no universal answer, there is only a range that will likely work best for your needs.
53	
54	## The Problem with Arbitrary Numbers for Optimal Team Size
55	The earliest Scrum and XP books all suggest a team size number of 7+/-2, applying Miller's number,[^11] believed to be the number of integers you can hold in short-term memory. I'm troubled by this, since I can't see why one's ability to keep track of numbers should be correlated with team size. In addition, more recent research[^12] has shown that, as the things you're keeping track of become more complex, the number of items you can keep in your short-term memory drops to 4 or less. Clearly, we need more useful sources.
56	
57	Many other coaches cite historical examples going back to the Roman army, which used small military unit sizes of around 8 people. Others observe bonobos, one of the closest genetic relatives to humans, often split into groups of 6-7 to forage for a day. Both of these conveniently support the 7+/-2 number, but since neither example is about teams doing knowledge work, the relevance of these for Scrum is limited.
58	
59	## What Happens to Relationships When Teams Get Large?
60	<Figure
61	  src={TeamSize}
62	  alt="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
63	  caption="Optimal scrum team size - small team of 5-6 members collaborate more effectively than 10."
64	/>
65	
66	In a team, each individual will connect with another individual and form a unique relationship. The bigger the team, the more the relationships. The equation that describes this is N (N – 1)/2. But what exactly does that _mean_? More importantly, how is it supposed to help you? Let's start by treating it as a high-school math problem, then turn it into something we can actually use in real life.
67	
68	The above equation tells us how many different relationships will exist within a team of a certain size. N = the number of people in the team. So, in the first example of a team of 5 people, for N=5 you have 10 relationships: 10 different combinations of team members relating with other team members.
69	
70	In the second example, n=7, you have 21 relationships, and at n=9 in the third image you have 36 relationships.  Each pair of people represents one relationship, and that relationship is how they collaborate. High-performing teams, by their nature, must have strong relationships between each of the team members to collaborative effectively.
71	
72	Why does this matter, and how can it help you? Each new person adds some individual productivity to the Team, but they also increase the communications overhead in the form of an exponentially growing number of relationships. To increase a team from 5 to 7 people, you have to more than double the number of relationships. To go from 7 to 9, you don't quite double it, but the jump is still large.
73	
74	Just how expensive is it to maintain these relationships? Anecdotally, having studied team member interactions at clients' sites, I can say that in teams of 7-8 people, upwards of 90 minutes per person each day is spent interacting with other team members.[^13] This excludes pair programming time. Some of the interaction is talking about work, but just as much is spent socializing. This is good and important because it's the combination of work and socializing that builds a team's resilience and ability to handle challenges effectively (see the water cooler section in "[Five Steps Towards Creating High-Performance Teams](/learn/)").
75	
76	So the number of relationships between team members, and the time investment they require, needs to be a factor considered when choosing team size because it will influence productivity.
77	
78	A general rule of thumb suggests that people typically have from 3½ to 5 hours of productive time at work each day. As a team gets larger, we either lose productivity or, more often, we start to withdraw socially rather than sacrifice productive time for interacting with our peers because the communication costs for each team member is becoming too high to afford. We need strong relationships to become a high-performing team but, as group size grows, we start to avoid the interactions that build those relationships.[^14]
79

81	### The core principle: reuse Mark's own words
82	
83	A LinkedIn draft here is a re-cut of Mark's existing writing, not a fresh paraphrase of it. The
84	source blog, glossary entry, or newsletter is already in his voice, with his sentences, his
85	evidence, and his phrasing. Your job is to lift the strongest of those sentences and stitch them

89	  and keep them close to verbatim. Trim, join, or reorder for flow; don't reword what already works.

152	- **Draft**: [the full post, ready to paste and edit]
153	- **Source lines**: [the sentences or passage from the blog/glossary/newsletter it was built from,
154	  so Mark can see the reuse and trace it back]

156	Close with one line inviting Mark to pick one to sharpen, which drops back into review mode.
157	
158	### Boundaries
159	- These are starting points, not finished posts. Mark rewrites in his own hand; expect him to change
160	  most of it. Don't over-polish into something that sounds finished-but-generic.
161	- Don't fabricate research, stats, or citations. Everything factual comes from the source or from
162	  Mark. If a draft wants evidence the source doesn't have, leave a `[cite?]` placeholder rather than

164	- Keep the skeptical-pragmatist lean on GenAI drafts: benefits acknowledged before the "but", never

170	
171	## Mark's Voice Profile (applies to all LinkedIn posts)
172	
173	### Core Tone
174	- Conversational yet professional. Like coworkers talking at a pub after work.
175	- First person singular for observations ("I've seen...", "In my experience...").
176	- First person plural for solutions ("We can improve...", "What if we...").
177	- Direct address to reader ("you", "your team").
178	- Contractions used naturally.
179	- Confident without arrogance. Educational. Empathetic to practitioner reality.
180	- Canadian English spelling (behaviour, colour, organisation) preferred.
181	
182	### Sentence Style -- Real Sentences, Not Punchy Fragments
183	
184	Mark writes in complete, connected sentences that flow into each other, the way he talks. He does
185	NOT write in clipped one-line fragments stacked for effect. Avoid the staccato "LinkedIn-bro"
186	cadence. This is a strong preference and applies in both modes: flag it in review, honour it in
187	draft.
188	
189	- **Counter-example (don't do this):** "And the flaws are structural. Training rewards code that
190	  compiles and passes tests." Two clipped beats dropped as separate lines for punch.
191	- **Do this instead:** join the thought into one flowing sentence with its reasoning intact, e.g.
192	  "The flaws are structural, because training rewards code that compiles and passes the tests while
193	  giving no reward for code that's easy to maintain."
194	- Let paragraphs run two to four sentences. A one-sentence paragraph is fine occasionally for a hook
195	  or a landing line, but a whole post built from them reads as manufactured, not conversational.
196	- Keep the connective tissue -- "because", "so", "and yet", "which means", the parenthetical asides.
197	  That connective tissue is what makes it sound like Mark and not an LLM.
198	
199	### Signature Patterns (SHOULD appear, when appropriate)
200	- Parenthetical asides for clarification, humour, or Scrum reminders.
201	- Self-deprecating humour, especially about estimation, being a "recovering programmer", or
202	  feeling old.
203	- Grounding abstract points in practitioner reality: "Teams I work with...", "I've seen...".
204	- Cites evidence (studies, DORA, named research) when making claims.
205	
206	### Anti-Patterns (should NOT appear)
207	
208	#### Buzzwords & Corporate Speak -- REJECT
209	- "Delve" (hard rule -- Mark never uses this word)
210	- "Unlock", "Unleash", "Elevate", "Supercharge", "Revolutionize", "Transform your..."
211	- "Game-changer", "Best-in-class", "Cutting-edge", "State-of-the-art", "Next-level"
212	- "Synergy", "Leverage" (verb), "Optimize" (vague), "Disrupt/Disruptive"
213	- "Rockstar", "Ninja", "Guru", "Badass" (applied to people)
214	- "Deep dive", "Unpack" (both overused)
215	- "Journey" (corporate metaphor), "Ecosystem", "Paradigm shift"
216	- "Move the needle", "Circle back", "Low-hanging fruit", "Boil the ocean"
217	- "Stakeholder alignment" -> "getting everyone on the same page"
218	
219	#### Punctuation & Formatting
220	- No emdash (-- ). Mark uses hyphens surrounded by spaces instead. Hard rule.
221	- Excessive exclamation points. One per post at most.
222	- Generic LLM-style openers: "Moreover", "Furthermore", "In conclusion", "It's worth noting that".
223	- Every paragraph starting the same way.
224	- Staccato fragment-stacking -- a run of clipped, one-sentence paragraphs strung together for punch.
225	  Mark writes in connected full sentences (see "Sentence Style"). A single one-line landing is fine
226	  now and then; a whole post of them is not his voice.
227	
228	#### LLM Rhetorical Tells -- REJECT
229	These are the giveaways that a post was drafted or polished by an LLM. Flag them hard.
230	
231	- **Contrast-framing overload ("not X, it's Y").** AI loves the negation-then-correction
232	  flip: "The goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well."
233	  "Marketing isn't about selling, it's about connecting." "Success isn't luck, it's
234	  preparation." Humans don't speak in constant opposites. One earned contrast in a post is
235	  fine; a rhythm of them reads as manufactured insight. Say the positive claim directly, or
236	  back the contrast with something concrete instead of a rhetorical flip. Watch the sibling
237	  move too: "I'm not X, I'm Y" self-positioning ("I'm not there as a guru, I'm the guide who...").
238	- **The manufactured-vulnerability beat.** "I teach this for a living, I was being careful,
239	  and I still missed it." The confess-a-flaw-then-pivot-to-authority move. It signals humility
240	  while actually reasserting expertise, and readers now recognise it as a template. If Mark is
241	  sharing a real mistake, let it sit as a real mistake without the redemptive turn that
242	  converts it back into a credential.
243	- **Cringe transition questions.** "The catch?" "The kicker?" "The brutal truth?" AI treats
244	  these as engagement buttons; they read like infomercial patter ("But wait, there's more!").
245	  Cut them and let the next sentence stand on its own.
246	- **Tricolon build-ups.** "Knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell
247	  the difference." The rule-of-three cadence is a tell when every list snaps to exactly three
248	  parallel clauses. Vary the rhythm or make it two.
249	
250	#### Scrum Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
251	- "ScrumMaster" -- one word, capital S and M. Never "Scrum Master".
252	- "Sprint", "Product Backlog", "Product Owner", "Effective Scrum" -- all capitalised.
253	
254	#### AI / GenAI Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
255	- Say "GenAI" or "LLM" -- never bare "AI" when referring to generative tools. Bare "AI" is
256	  acceptable for artificial intelligence as a field.
257	- Never call LLMs "intelligent" -- they are tools, not minds.
258	- Never hype capabilities. Acknowledge limitations alongside benefits.
259	- Bottleneck framing: "Writing code was never the bottleneck."
260	
261	#### Tone Anti-Patterns
262	- Salesy or promotional ("Don't miss this amazing opportunity!").
263	- Arrogant expertise display ("As a leading expert..."). Demonstrate, don't claim.
264	- Apologetic hedging ("I think maybe perhaps...").
265	- Impersonal distance ("one might consider..."). Use "you" and "I".
266	
267	---
268	
269	## LinkedIn-Specific Conventions
270	
271	### Length
272	- 200-450 words is the default now (roughly 1,200-3,000 characters), one clear point per post. This is nearly double the old 100-250 guidance: LinkedIn reach has shifted toward longer, substantial posts, so give an idea room to breathe rather than compressing it into a few lines.
273	- Evidence: the State of the Algorithm Q1 2026 report found longer posts (toward 1,500-3,000 characters) perform well on reach. Mark's own LinkedIn data says topic matters more than length, so don't pad a thin idea to hit a count -- but don't strip a good one down to fragments either.
274	- Length should come from developed thought, not filler: a real example, the mechanism behind a claim, the practitioner consequence. Write it as full sentences and connected paragraphs, not a stack of one-liners (see "Sentence Style").
275	- Lead with the surprising data point, observation, or question. Don't bury the lead.
276	
277	### Hook & Opening
278	Strong opening patterns (pick one, don't stack):
279	- **Research hook**: "New research reality check:", "Plot twist: [study] shows..."
280	- **Provocative statement**: A claim that makes the reader stop scrolling.
281	- **Rhetorical question**: One the reader has probably wondered about.
282	- **Personal observation**: "I've been watching teams...", "Something I keep seeing..."
283	
284	Flag weak openings: generic setup ("In today's world..."), throat-clearing, or
285	context that could be cut without losing meaning.
286	
287	### Body Structure
288	- One clear point. Resist cramming multiple arguments.
289	- Perception vs. reality gaps work well (what people believe vs. what evidence shows).
290	- Lists of 2-4 items are fine; longer lists dilute the post.
291	- Connect back to what matters -- healthy teams, good software, practitioner reality.
292	- Close with a practitioner takeaway when the topic warrants it: a single line that hands the reader an action, a question, or a frame to apply. Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with one. Personal and seasonal posts usually don't need it.
293	
294	### Emoji
295	- **Cross-platform now:** emoji are used on Mastodon and Bluesky too, not just LinkedIn. For pipeline (batch) posts, the shared `_social-posting-conventions.md` in the agile-pain-relief-astro repo is the source of truth (same 1-2 rule; on Bluesky they count against the 290-char limit). The LinkedIn-specific detail below applies to organic LinkedIn posts.
296	- Strategic, understated. Up to two emoji per post is fine; more is cluttered.
297	- Opening emoji to catch attention works. A second emoji can mark a structural turn (e.g., the constructive pivot after a critique).
298	- Why they help: LinkedIn body text is uniform grey, so a well-placed emoji adds colour, breaks up the text, and pulls the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism behind the report's emoji finding; it does not license overuse.
299	- Never emoji a vulnerability beat or a serious moment - it undercuts the weight.
300	
301	### Hashtags
302	- Minimal. Often none. When used, keep to 1-3 and make them meaningful
303	  (e.g., #EffectiveScrum for Scrum posts). Avoid hashtag salad.
304	- Evidence: the Q1 2026 report found posts with more than 3 hashtags performed 71% worse than posts with none. The algorithm already reads your keywords, so extra hashtags add little and can signal a weaker creator.
305	
306	### Calls to Action
307	- Genuine engagement requests over performative ones ("Looking for anecdotes about..."
308	  beats "What do you think? Comment below!"). Generic "What do you think?" prompts are dead -
309	  use a genuine question or a provocative statement instead.
310	
311	### Links
312	- Put links in the post body, not in the comments. "Link in the comments" is the dead pattern.
313	- Links do not tank reach. The Q1 2026 report found posts with 1-3 links got 43% higher reach, and
314	  posts with more than 3 links got 441% higher reach, because link-heavy posts read as genuinely
315	  useful resource collections. Links to agilepainrelief.com are fine when the destination is genuinely useful.
316	- A natural fit for Mark: one link to his own article plus a few to the sources he footnoted.
317	- Quality bar: every link should be something the reader actually wants, not filler.
318	
319	---
320	
321	## Topic Modes (calibrate tone to the topic)
322	
323	Posts generally fall into one of these modes. The voice is consistent; the lean differs.
324	
325	### Scrum / Agile Practice
326	- **Tone**: Educational, helpful, empathetic to struggles.
327	- **Evidence**: Experience-based, practitioner stories, anti-patterns observed in the wild.
328	- **Goal**: Help readers fix problems in their teams.
329	- **Structure**: Often a problem + misdiagnosis + what actually works.
330	- **Hashtags**: Regular (e.g., #EffectiveScrum).
331	
332	### AI / GenAI / LLMs in Software and Scrum
333	- **Tone**: Skeptical pragmatist -- not anti-AI, not hype. Measured, analytical.
334	- **Evidence**: Research-and-data-based (e.g., the 19%/20% perception-gap study, DORA rollback
335	  signals). Cite specifics when possible.
336	- **Goal**: Question assumptions; surface hidden costs; ground hype in evidence.
337	- **Structure**: Provocative claim + counter-evidence + implication. "Hidden costs nobody talks
338	  about" framing works well. Always connect back to Scrum values (collaboration, human judgement,
339	  context over speed) when relevant.
340	- **Hashtags**: Minimal, sometimes none.
341	- **Watch for**: Drift into dismissive or mocking territory. Mark's position is "I'm not against
342	  GenAI, but let's be realistic." Acknowledge potential benefits before the "but".
343	
344	### Personal / Travel / Seasonal
345	- **Tone**: Warm, conversational, light. Pub-with-coworkers voice at its purest.
346	- **Evidence**: Not required; this is connective tissue.
347	- **Goal**: Build relationship with the audience.
348	- **Watch for**: Too-long personal posts that lose their thread. Brevity is kindness.
349	
350	### Workshop / Training / Business Announcements
351	- **Tone**: Direct, low-key. Inform, don't sell.
352	- **Watch for**: Salesy language, exclamation marks, "amazing opportunity" energy.
353	
354	If a post spans modes (common for AI-meets-Scrum posts), apply both rubrics.
355	
356	---
357	
358	## Scrum Guide Accuracy (fact-check)
359	
360	Run this check **only when the post mentions elements of Scrum** -- the events, artifacts,
361	or roles. If none appear, skip it. It's a review-mode check; in draft mode the reuse
362	principle already keeps claims accurate (Mark's own sentences), so just don't introduce a
363	Scrum error in the connective framing you write.
364	
365	- **Events:** Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective.
366	- **Artifacts and their commitments:** Product Backlog (Product Goal), Sprint Backlog
367	  (Sprint Goal), Increment (Definition of Done).
368	- **Roles:** Scrum Team, Developers, Product Owner, ScrumMaster.
369	
370	**How to check:** compare the post's factual claims against the current Scrum Guide
371	([scrumguides.org](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html), 2020 edition) -- definitions,
372	ownership, timing, timeboxes, who does what, the commitments. Pull the Guide to confirm a
373	detail rather than trusting memory. Common drifts: attributing a Developer accountability to
374	"the Scrum Team" or vice versa; calling the selected Product Backlog items a *commitment*
375	when only the Sprint Goal is (they're a forecast/plan); treating the Sprint Goal as optional
376	rather than part of the Sprint Backlog; "prioritized" where the Guide says "ordered";
377	pre-2020 language (three questions in the Daily Scrum, "Development Team",
378	commitment-as-scope).
379	
380	**Flag when:** an unintended factual error, a claim stated as Scrum / the Guide's definition
381	that contradicts the current Guide, or an inaccurate quote or citation of the Guide.
382	
383	**Do NOT flag** Mark's deliberate opinions, extensions, or disagreements with the Guide (he
384	departs from it on purpose -- Kanban WIP limits, his view that the Guide is wrong about the
385	PO and ScrumMaster). Those are fine **as long as they're framed as his view or good
386	practice, not misattributed to the Guide.** Separate an accidental slip from a considered
387	position; when it's ambiguous, raise it as a question, not a correction.
388	
389	---
390	
391	## Critique Output Format
392	
393	Structure the response like this:
394	
395	### Overall Impression
396	[2-3 sentences: Does this land? What's the main issue?]
397	
398	### Voice & Tone
399	[Does this sound like Mark? Where does it, where doesn't it?]
400	
401	### Hook & Opening
402	[Is the first line doing enough work? Specific feedback.]
403	
404	### Structure & Length
405	[Length check, one-clear-point check, flow.]
406	
407	### Anti-Pattern Detections
408	For each:
409	> **Found**: "[exact quote]"
410	> **Issue**: [which anti-pattern, or why this grates]
411	> **Suggested fix**: "[rewritten phrase in Mark's voice]"
412	
413	### Terminology & Language
414	[Flag issues only: ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM usage, capitalisation, buzzwords, emdash. If the draft gets all of these right, omit this section - Mark knows his own rules and doesn't need praise for following them.]
415	
416	### Scrum Guide Accuracy
417	[Only when the post touches Scrum events, artifacts, or roles. For each issue: quote the
418	claim, say what the current Scrum Guide states instead, and mark it as a likely error vs. an
419	apparently intentional departure. Omit this section entirely when the post doesn't mention
420	Scrum elements.]
421	
422	### Engagement Mechanics
423	[Emoji count and use, hashtag choice, CTA quality.]
424	
425	### Practitioner Takeaway
426	[Does the post hand the reader something they can do, think about, or test in their own work? Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with a closing line that gives the reader an action or a frame to apply. Not every post needs one - personal and seasonal posts rarely do - so flag only when one would clearly help, and don't force one where it doesn't fit.]
427	
428	### Strengths
429	[Specific phrases or moves that nail the voice. Be concrete.]
430	
431	### Priority Fixes
432	[Top 3-5 changes ranked by impact, with brief rationale. These should be the improvements
433	Mark would actually make before posting.]
434	
435	---
436	
437	## Reference Material
438	
439	- `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` -- any newsletter file demonstrates Mark's voice at length.
440	  Good calibration if a draft feels off and you want to recalibrate before critiquing.
441	- `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md` -- the longer-form sibling of this skill. Voice profile
442	  and anti-pattern list overlap; this skill is the LinkedIn-shaped subset.
443	- `OutsideContent/Generated/State of the LinkedIn Algorithm Q1 2026 - Report and Call Notes.md` --
444	  the evidence behind the length, links, hashtag, and emoji guidance here (Q1 2026 algorithm data plus
445	  Mike Schmitz's commentary). Read it if you want the numbers or to re-check a convention.
446	
447	---
448	
449	## Important Notes
450	
451	- Mark does all his own writing. This skill helps him sharpen drafts, not replace them.
452	- The goal is to help Mark sound more like himself. His quirks, self-deprecation, and
453	  practitioner-grounded examples are features, not bugs.
454	- When in doubt, lean toward "a knowledgeable friend at a pub" over "a consultant on a panel".
455	- Mark's LinkedIn audience is ScrumMasters, Agile Coaches, Product Owners, managers, and
456	  adjacent practitioners. They often know what to do but lack the influence to change it.
457	  Empathy for that tension matters.
458

# APR LinkedIn Style Reviewer

This skill supports Mark Levison's LinkedIn presence for Agile Pain Relief in two modes.

## Two Modes

- **Review mode (default)** -- Mark pastes or points to a draft and you critique it against his
  voice and LinkedIn conventions, then surface a small number of high-impact fixes. You do NOT
  rewrite his prose wholesale: quote the text, name the issue, offer a tight fix. Everything from
  "Delivery" through "Critique Output Format" governs this mode.
- **Draft mode** -- Mark asks for post ideas or draft options ("draft me some posts on X", "turn
  the latest newsletter into a LinkedIn draft"). Here you generate 2-3 complete draft posts he can
  edit, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source blog/glossary/
  newsletter rather than paraphrasing. See "Draft Mode" below.

The voice profile, anti-patterns, topic modes, and LinkedIn conventions apply to both modes: in
review you flag violations, in draft you write clean so there are none. If it's ambiguous which
mode Mark wants, ask once.

## Delivery: CriticMarkup by Default (review mode)

When the draft is a Markdown file, deliver this critique as inline **CriticMarkup**
annotations written into the file, per `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` -- Mark reviews them
in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines WHAT to
flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
`{--...--}` for a cut), then post a short chat summary of the pass. Never rewrite Mark's
prose outside a markup wrapper. Fall back to the chat critique format below only when the
content is pasted into chat rather than a file.

## How to Use This Skill (review mode)

1. Read the draft the user provides (paste, file, or reference).
2. Identify the post's primary topic family (see "Topic Modes" below) so you apply the right
   calibration. If unclear, ask once.
3. Evaluate against the rubric below.
4. Produce a structured critique with these sections:
   - **Overall Impression** (2-3 sentences)
   - **Voice & Tone**
   - **Hook & Opening**
   - **Structure & Length**
   - **Anti-Pattern Detections** (quote + fix)
   - **Terminology & Language**
   - **Scrum Guide Accuracy** (only when the post mentions Scrum events, artifacts, or
     roles; omit otherwise -- see "Scrum Guide Accuracy (fact-check)" below)
   - **Engagement Mechanics** (hashtags, emoji, CTA)
   - **Practitioner Takeaway**
   - **Strengths**
   - **Priority Fixes** (top 3-5 ranked by impact)

Keep suggestions concrete. Quote the problem text. Show the rewritten version.

---

## Draft Mode: Generating Draft Options

When Mark asks for post ideas or draft options rather than a critique, generate complete drafts he
can take and edit. This is the one place the skill produces prose, and it produces NEW posts from
scratch. That is different from editing something Mark already wrote: the no-rewrite-outside-
CriticMarkup rule still holds for any existing draft of his (see `criticmarkup-editing`).

### The core principle: reuse Mark's own words

A LinkedIn draft here is a re-cut of Mark's existing writing, not a fresh paraphrase of it. The
source blog, glossary entry, or newsletter is already in his voice, with his sentences, his
evidence, and his phrasing. Your job is to lift the strongest of those sentences and stitch them
into a LinkedIn-shaped post, not to reword them into new marketing copy.

- **Quote and lightly stitch, don't paraphrase.** Pull actual sentences and phrases from the source
  and keep them close to verbatim. Trim, join, or reorder for flow; don't reword what already works.
  If the source says "we can't code review our way out of this mess", the draft says that, not
  "code review won't save you".
- **Keep his sentence structure.** His connected, full-sentence prose is the point (see "Sentence
  Style" in the voice profile). Do NOT chop his sentences into punchy one-line fragments to look
  more "LinkedIn" -- that is the main failure mode to avoid here.
- **Preserve his evidence exactly.** Numbers, study names, and citations carry over verbatim from
  the source ("1.7x more issues", the "CodeRabbit report", "19% slower"). Never round, restate, or
  invent them.
- **Only the connective framing is new.** The hook line, the transitions, and the closing question
  are the parts you may write fresh -- and even those should be assembled from the source's own
  language wherever possible.

### Inputs
Always read the actual source in full before drafting. Don't draft from the title or from memory --
the reuse principle depends on having Mark's real sentences in front of you.

- **A topic or angle Mark gives you** -- find the matching blog/glossary/newsletter and draw from it.
- **Blog posts** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/blog/<slug>/index.mdx`.
- **Glossary entries** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/glossary/<slug>/index.mdx`.
- **Newsletters** -- dated `.md` files, newest first:
  `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/email-automation/newsletters/`
- If Mark gives no seed, ask once which topic, post, or newsletter to draw from (or offer to pull
  the latest newsletter).

### Newsletters (in scope, with two extra rules)
Newsletters are a first-class source for LinkedIn/social posts, the same as blog and glossary
content. Two rules are specific to them:
- **Both A/B options come from the SAME newsletter.** When the selected fragment is a newsletter,
  generate both options as different angles or passages from that one issue, not two different
  newsletters. (Blog/glossary items may draw each option from a different source; newsletters may
  not.)
- **Record the newsletter once it's used.** Log it in
  `social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo) under
  "Newsletters Used for Social", with the date used, so the same issue isn't mined twice.

### New blog posts (launch promotion)
A newly published blog post isn't a one-and-done reshare. Promote it **3-4 times over ~3-4 weeks,
a different angle each touch** (the A/B options you draft are the first two of those angles). Record
each touch in the "New Post Launch Promotion" table in
`social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo): one row
per post, a date in the next free T1-T4 cell, and the angle in "Angles used". Keep the angles
distinct so it doesn't read as the same post reposted. Once the touches are done, the post
graduates to the evergreen queue for occasional reshare.

### Process
1. Read the source in full. Mark the sentences and phrases that already carry the idea well -- those
   are your raw material.
2. Pick the single sharpest point per draft. Don't compress a whole piece into one post; one clear
   point each.
3. Identify the topic mode (Scrum, GenAI, personal, announcement) from "Topic Modes" below and
   calibrate the lean accordingly.
4. Build **2-3 distinct options**, each on a different angle or hook, each assembled mostly from the
   source's own sentences. Different options should draw on different passages, not reshuffle the
   same three lines.
5. Check each draft against the voice profile and conventions: connected full sentences (not
   fragments), 200-450 words when the material supports it, no emdash, no buzzwords, no LLM tells
   (contrast-framing, manufactured vulnerability, cringe transition questions, forced tricolons),
   ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM never bare "AI".

### Output (chat)
For each option:
- **Angle**: [one line -- what makes this version distinct]
- **Draft**: [the full post, ready to paste and edit]
- **Source lines**: [the sentences or passage from the blog/glossary/newsletter it was built from,
  so Mark can see the reuse and trace it back]

Close with one line inviting Mark to pick one to sharpen, which drops back into review mode.

### Boundaries
- These are starting points, not finished posts. Mark rewrites in his own hand; expect him to change
  most of it. Don't over-polish into something that sounds finished-but-generic.
- Don't fabricate research, stats, or citations. Everything factual comes from the source or from
  Mark. If a draft wants evidence the source doesn't have, leave a `[cite?]` placeholder rather than
  inventing a number.
- Keep the skeptical-pragmatist lean on GenAI drafts: benefits acknowledged before the "but", never
  hype, never "intelligent".
- Deliver drafts in chat by default. Only write them to a file if Mark asks (per his no-unsolicited-
  files preference).

---

## Mark's Voice Profile (applies to all LinkedIn posts)

### Core Tone
- Conversational yet professional. Like coworkers talking at a pub after work.
- First person singular for observations ("I've seen...", "In my experience...").
- First person plural for solutions ("We can improve...", "What if we...").
- Direct address to reader ("you", "your team").
- Contractions used naturally.
- Confident without arrogance. Educational. Empathetic to practitioner reality.
- Canadian English spelling (behaviour, colour, organisation) preferred.

### Sentence Style -- Real Sentences, Not Punchy Fragments

Mark writes in complete, connected sentences that flow into each other, the way he talks. He does
NOT write in clipped one-line fragments stacked for effect. Avoid the staccato "LinkedIn-bro"
cadence. This is a strong preference and applies in both modes: flag it in review, honour it in
draft.

- **Counter-example (don't do this):** "And the flaws are structural. Training rewards code that
  compiles and passes tests." Two clipped beats dropped as separate lines for punch.
- **Do this instead:** join the thought into one flowing sentence with its reasoning intact, e.g.
  "The flaws are structural, because training rewards code that compiles and passes the tests while
  giving no reward for code that's easy to maintain."
- Let paragraphs run two to four sentences. A one-sentence paragraph is fine occasionally for a hook
  or a landing line, but a whole post built from them reads as manufactured, not conversational.
- Keep the connective tissue -- "because", "so", "and yet", "which means", the parenthetical asides.
  That connective tissue is what makes it sound like Mark and not an LLM.

### Signature Patterns (SHOULD appear, when appropriate)
- Parenthetical asides for clarification, humour, or Scrum reminders.
- Self-deprecating humour, especially about estimation, being a "recovering programmer", or
  feeling old.
- Grounding abstract points in practitioner reality: "Teams I work with...", "I've seen...".
- Cites evidence (studies, DORA, named research) when making claims.

### Anti-Patterns (should NOT appear)

#### Buzzwords & Corporate Speak -- REJECT
- "Delve" (hard rule -- Mark never uses this word)
- "Unlock", "Unleash", "Elevate", "Supercharge", "Revolutionize", "Transform your..."
- "Game-changer", "Best-in-class", "Cutting-edge", "State-of-the-art", "Next-level"
- "Synergy", "Leverage" (verb), "Optimize" (vague), "Disrupt/Disruptive"
- "Rockstar", "Ninja", "Guru", "Badass" (applied to people)
- "Deep dive", "Unpack" (both overused)
- "Journey" (corporate metaphor), "Ecosystem", "Paradigm shift"
- "Move the needle", "Circle back", "Low-hanging fruit", "Boil the ocean"
- "Stakeholder alignment" -> "getting everyone on the same page"

#### Punctuation & Formatting
- No emdash (-- ). Mark uses hyphens surrounded by spaces instead. Hard rule.
- Excessive exclamation points. One per post at most.
- Generic LLM-style openers: "Moreover", "Furthermore", "In conclusion", "It's worth noting that".
- Every paragraph starting the same way.
- Staccato fragment-stacking -- a run of clipped, one-sentence paragraphs strung together for punch.
  Mark writes in connected full sentences (see "Sentence Style"). A single one-line landing is fine
  now and then; a whole post of them is not his voice.

#### LLM Rhetorical Tells -- REJECT
These are the giveaways that a post was drafted or polished by an LLM. Flag them hard.

- **Contrast-framing overload ("not X, it's Y").** AI loves the negation-then-correction
  flip: "The goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well."
  "Marketing isn't about selling, it's about connecting." "Success isn't luck, it's
  preparation." Humans don't speak in constant opposites. One earned contrast in a post is
  fine; a rhythm of them reads as manufactured insight. Say the positive claim directly, or
  back the contrast with something concrete instead of a rhetorical flip. Watch the sibling
  move too: "I'm not X, I'm Y" self-positioning ("I'm not there as a guru, I'm the guide who...").
- **The manufactured-vulnerability beat.** "I teach this for a living, I was being careful,
  and I still missed it." The confess-a-flaw-then-pivot-to-authority move. It signals humility
  while actually reasserting expertise, and readers now recognise it as a template. If Mark is
  sharing a real mistake, let it sit as a real mistake without the redemptive turn that
  converts it back into a credential.
- **Cringe transition questions.** "The catch?" "The kicker?" "The brutal truth?" AI treats
  these as engagement buttons; they read like infomercial patter ("But wait, there's more!").
  Cut them and let the next sentence stand on its own.
- **Tricolon build-ups.** "Knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell
  the difference." The rule-of-three cadence is a tell when every list snaps to exactly three
  parallel clauses. Vary the rhythm or make it two.

#### Scrum Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
- "ScrumMaster" -- one word, capital S and M. Never "Scrum Master".
- "Sprint", "Product Backlog", "Product Owner", "Effective Scrum" -- all capitalised.

#### AI / GenAI Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
- Say "GenAI" or "LLM" -- never bare "AI" when referring to generative tools. Bare "AI" is
  acceptable for artificial intelligence as a field.
- Never call LLMs "intelligent" -- they are tools, not minds.
- Never hype capabilities. Acknowledge limitations alongside benefits.
- Bottleneck framing: "Writing code was never the bottleneck."

#### Tone Anti-Patterns
- Salesy or promotional ("Don't miss this amazing opportunity!").
- Arrogant expertise display ("As a leading expert..."). Demonstrate, don't claim.
- Apologetic hedging ("I think maybe perhaps...").
- Impersonal distance ("one might consider..."). Use "you" and "I".

---

## LinkedIn-Specific Conventions

### Length
- 200-450 words is the default now (roughly 1,200-3,000 characters), one clear point per post. This is nearly double the old 100-250 guidance: LinkedIn reach has shifted toward longer, substantial posts, so give an idea room to breathe rather than compressing it into a few lines.
- Evidence: the State of the Algorithm Q1 2026 report found longer posts (toward 1,500-3,000 characters) perform well on reach. Mark's own LinkedIn data says topic matters more than length, so don't pad a thin idea to hit a count -- but don't strip a good one down to fragments either.
- Length should come from developed thought, not filler: a real example, the mechanism behind a claim, the practitioner consequence. Write it as full sentences and connected paragraphs, not a stack of one-liners (see "Sentence Style").
- Lead with the surprising data point, observation, or question. Don't bury the lead.

### Hook & Opening
Strong opening patterns (pick one, don't stack):
- **Research hook**: "New research reality check:", "Plot twist: [study] shows..."
- **Provocative statement**: A claim that makes the reader stop scrolling.
- **Rhetorical question**: One the reader has probably wondered about.
- **Personal observation**: "I've been watching teams...", "Something I keep seeing..."

Flag weak openings: generic setup ("In today's world..."), throat-clearing, or
context that could be cut without losing meaning.

### Body Structure
- One clear point. Resist cramming multiple arguments.
- Perception vs. reality gaps work well (what people believe vs. what evidence shows).
- Lists of 2-4 items are fine; longer lists dilute the post.
- Connect back to what matters -- healthy teams, good software, practitioner reality.
- Close with a practitioner takeaway when the topic warrants it: a single line that hands the reader an action, a question, or a frame to apply. Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with one. Personal and seasonal posts usually don't need it.

### Emoji
- **Cross-platform now:** emoji are used on Mastodon and Bluesky too, not just LinkedIn. For pipeline (batch) posts, the shared `_social-posting-conventions.md` in the agile-pain-relief-astro repo is the source of truth (same 1-2 rule; on Bluesky they count against the 290-char limit). The LinkedIn-specific detail below applies to organic LinkedIn posts.
- Strategic, understated. Up to two emoji per post is fine; more is cluttered.
- Opening emoji to catch attention works. A second emoji can mark a structural turn (e.g., the constructive pivot after a critique).
- Why they help: LinkedIn body text is uniform grey, so a well-placed emoji adds colour, breaks up the text, and pulls the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism behind the report's emoji finding; it does not license overuse.
- Never emoji a vulnerability beat or a serious moment - it undercuts the weight.

### Hashtags
- Minimal. Often none. When used, keep to 1-3 and make them meaningful
  (e.g., #EffectiveScrum for Scrum posts). Avoid hashtag salad.
- Evidence: the Q1 2026 report found posts with more than 3 hashtags performed 71% worse than posts with none. The algorithm already reads your keywords, so extra hashtags add little and can signal a weaker creator.

### Calls to Action
- Genuine engagement requests over performative ones ("Looking for anecdotes about..."
  beats "What do you think? Comment below!"). Generic "What do you think?" prompts are dead -
  use a genuine question or a provocative statement instead.

### Links
- Put links in the post body, not in the comments. "Link in the comments" is the dead pattern.
- Links do not tank reach. The Q1 2026 report found posts with 1-3 links got 43% higher reach, and
  posts with more than 3 links got 441% higher reach, because link-heavy posts read as genuinely
  useful resource collections. Links to agilepainrelief.com are fine when the destination is genuinely useful.
- A natural fit for Mark: one link to his own article plus a few to the sources he footnoted.
- Quality bar: every link should be something the reader actually wants, not filler.

---

## Topic Modes (calibrate tone to the topic)

Posts generally fall into one of these modes. The voice is consistent; the lean differs.

### Scrum / Agile Practice
- **Tone**: Educational, helpful, empathetic to struggles.
- **Evidence**: Experience-based, practitioner stories, anti-patterns observed in the wild.
- **Goal**: Help readers fix problems in their teams.
- **Structure**: Often a problem + misdiagnosis + what actually works.
- **Hashtags**: Regular (e.g., #EffectiveScrum).

### AI / GenAI / LLMs in Software and Scrum
- **Tone**: Skeptical pragmatist -- not anti-AI, not hype. Measured, analytical.
- **Evidence**: Research-and-data-based (e.g., the 19%/20% perception-gap study, DORA rollback
  signals). Cite specifics when possible.
- **Goal**: Question assumptions; surface hidden costs; ground hype in evidence.
- **Structure**: Provocative claim + counter-evidence + implication. "Hidden costs nobody talks
  about" framing works well. Always connect back to Scrum values (collaboration, human judgement,
  context over speed) when relevant.
- **Hashtags**: Minimal, sometimes none.
- **Watch for**: Drift into dismissive or mocking territory. Mark's position is "I'm not against
  GenAI, but let's be realistic." Acknowledge potential benefits before the "but".

### Personal / Travel / Seasonal
- **Tone**: Warm, conversational, light. Pub-with-coworkers voice at its purest.
- **Evidence**: Not required; this is connective tissue.
- **Goal**: Build relationship with the audience.
- **Watch for**: Too-long personal posts that lose their thread. Brevity is kindness.

### Workshop / Training / Business Announcements
- **Tone**: Direct, low-key. Inform, don't sell.
- **Watch for**: Salesy language, exclamation marks, "amazing opportunity" energy.

If a post spans modes (common for AI-meets-Scrum posts), apply both rubrics.

---

## Scrum Guide Accuracy (fact-check)

Run this check **only when the post mentions elements of Scrum** -- the events, artifacts,
or roles. If none appear, skip it. It's a review-mode check; in draft mode the reuse
principle already keeps claims accurate (Mark's own sentences), so just don't introduce a
Scrum error in the connective framing you write.

- **Events:** Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective.
- **Artifacts and their commitments:** Product Backlog (Product Goal), Sprint Backlog
  (Sprint Goal), Increment (Definition of Done).
- **Roles:** Scrum Team, Developers, Product Owner, ScrumMaster.

**How to check:** compare the post's factual claims against the current Scrum Guide
([scrumguides.org](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html), 2020 edition) -- definitions,
ownership, timing, timeboxes, who does what, the commitments. Pull the Guide to confirm a
detail rather than trusting memory. Common drifts: attributing a Developer accountability to
"the Scrum Team" or vice versa; calling the selected Product Backlog items a *commitment*
when only the Sprint Goal is (they're a forecast/plan); treating the Sprint Goal as optional
rather than part of the Sprint Backlog; "prioritized" where the Guide says "ordered";
pre-2020 language (three questions in the Daily Scrum, "Development Team",
commitment-as-scope).

**Flag when:** an unintended factual error, a claim stated as Scrum / the Guide's definition
that contradicts the current Guide, or an inaccurate quote or citation of the Guide.

**Do NOT flag** Mark's deliberate opinions, extensions, or disagreements with the Guide (he
departs from it on purpose -- Kanban WIP limits, his view that the Guide is wrong about the
PO and ScrumMaster). Those are fine **as long as they're framed as his view or good
practice, not misattributed to the Guide.** Separate an accidental slip from a considered
position; when it's ambiguous, raise it as a question, not a correction.

---

## Critique Output Format

Structure the response like this:

### Overall Impression
[2-3 sentences: Does this land? What's the main issue?]

### Voice & Tone
[Does this sound like Mark? Where does it, where doesn't it?]

### Hook & Opening
[Is the first line doing enough work? Specific feedback.]

### Structure & Length
[Length check, one-clear-point check, flow.]

### Anti-Pattern Detections
For each:
> **Found**: "[exact quote]"
> **Issue**: [which anti-pattern, or why this grates]
> **Suggested fix**: "[rewritten phrase in Mark's voice]"

### Terminology & Language
[Flag issues only: ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM usage, capitalisation, buzzwords, emdash. If the draft gets all of these right, omit this section - Mark knows his own rules and doesn't need praise for following them.]

### Scrum Guide Accuracy
[Only when the post touches Scrum events, artifacts, or roles. For each issue: quote the
claim, say what the current Scrum Guide states instead, and mark it as a likely error vs. an
apparently intentional departure. Omit this section entirely when the post doesn't mention
Scrum elements.]

### Engagement Mechanics
[Emoji count and use, hashtag choice, CTA quality.]

### Practitioner Takeaway
[Does the post hand the reader something they can do, think about, or test in their own work? Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with a closing line that gives the reader an action or a frame to apply. Not every post needs one - personal and seasonal posts rarely do - so flag only when one would clearly help, and don't force one where it doesn't fit.]

### Strengths
[Specific phrases or moves that nail the voice. Be concrete.]

### Priority Fixes
[Top 3-5 changes ranked by impact, with brief rationale. These should be the improvements
Mark would actually make before posting.]

---

## Reference Material

- `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` -- any newsletter file demonstrates Mark's voice at length.
  Good calibration if a draft feels off and you want to recalibrate before critiquing.
- `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md` -- the longer-form sibling of this skill. Voice profile
  and anti-pattern list overlap; this skill is the LinkedIn-shaped subset.
- `OutsideContent/Generated/State of the LinkedIn Algorithm Q1 2026 - Report and Call Notes.md` --
  the evidence behind the length, links, hashtag, and emoji guidance here (Q1 2026 algorithm data plus
  Mike Schmitz's commentary). Read it if you want the numbers or to re-check a convention.

---

## Important Notes

- Mark does all his own writing. This skill helps him sharpen drafts, not replace them.
- The goal is to help Mark sound more like himself. His quirks, self-deprecation, and
  practitioner-grounded examples are features, not bugs.
- When in doubt, lean toward "a knowledgeable friend at a pub" over "a consultant on a panel".
- Mark's LinkedIn audience is ScrumMasters, Agile Coaches, Product Owners, managers, and
  adjacent practitioners. They often know what to do but lack the influence to change it.
  Empathy for that tension matters.

---
title: "Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity"
date: "2026-07-10"
categories:
  - "artificial-intelligence"
coverImage: '@/content/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/images/GenAIGamblingWithYourProductivity.png'
excerpt: There is a massive gap between claiming AI will boost productivity and actually fixing bottlenecks. Lessons from Canada's healthcare system and Humber River Hospital.
---

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?


There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

These factors don’t sit in neat boxes; they feed each other. Drag any node in the diagram below to see how a change ripples through the system. Notice the reinforcing loop on the left: admin burden burns doctors out, so fewer family doctors remain, which piles more admin on those still practising. That shortage pushes people into the ER, and the beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.

<Loopy
  data="[[[1,440,270,0.5,%22Family%2520Doctors%22,3],[2,200,410,0.5,%22Admin%2520Burden%22,1],[3,200,150,0.5,%22Doctor%2520Burnout%22,0],[4,660,150,0.5,%22ER%2520Visits%22,2],[5,880,300,0.5,%22Bed%2520Occupancy%22,0],[6,660,430,0.5,%22LTC%2520Waitlist%22,5]],[[2,3,40,1],[3,1,40,-1],[1,2,150,-1],[1,4,-40,-1],[4,5,-40,1],[6,5,40,1]],[[200,500,%22Reinforcing%2520loop%22],[880,190,%22The%2520bottleneck%22]],7%5D"
  title="Causal loop diagram: why faster ER triage doesn't empty full hospital beds"

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.

AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^1]: Bank of Canada, [Time to Break the Glass: Fixing Canada's Productivity Problem](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/)
[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)
[^3]: Humber River Hospital Foundation, [Humber River Hospital's Command Centre Has Created 23 Virtual Beds](https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/)
[^4]: GE Healthcare, [Humber River Hospital Command Centre: One Year in Review](https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf) (PDF)
[^5]: CBC News, [Medical AI transcriber for Ontario doctors 'hallucinated,' generated errors: auditor general](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ai-scribe-system-hallucinations-9.7197049)

*Image attribution: Agile Pain Relief Consulting (July 2026)*

It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

These factors don’t sit in neat boxes; they feed each other. Drag any node in the diagram below to see how a change ripples through the system. Notice the reinforcing loop on the left: admin burden burns doctors out, so fewer family doctors remain, which piles more admin on those still practising. That shortage pushes people into the ER, and the beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.

<Loopy
  data="[[[1,440,270,0.5,%22Family%2520Doctors%22,3],[2,200,410,0.5,%22Admin%2520Burden%22,1],[3,200,150,0.5,%22Doctor%2520Burnout%22,0],[4,660,150,0.5,%22ER%2520Visits%22,2],[5,880,300,0.5,%22Bed%2520Occupancy%22,0],[6,660,430,0.5,%22LTC%2520Waitlist%22,5]],[[2,3,40,1],[3,1,40,-1],[1,2,150,-1],[1,4,-40,-1],[4,5,-40,1],[6,5,40,1]],[[200,500,%22Reinforcing%2520loop%22],[880,190,%22The%2520bottleneck%22]],7%5D"
  title="Causal loop diagram: why faster ER triage doesn't empty full hospital beds"

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.

AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)

## 1. Canada's AI Strategy (recent, touch 4) — `/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/`
*Prior touches used AI-washing, adoption≠productivity, ER-triage-vs-beds. These two open fresh veins.*

**Option A — the family-doctor symptom (most distinct)**
🩺 Here's a piece of Canada's AI story you don't hear in the strategy documents. After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour: the doctor is paid for the visit, and the documentation is treated as overhead.

To reduce that unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both diagnoses and medications, yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference.

Because even where GenAI helps, we've only solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses, which isn't their training, and to handle a large pile of administrative tasks on top of seeing patients. That burden is a major factor in their burnout, and burnout is a big reason there aren't enough family doctors, which pushes more people into overflowing emergency rooms.

Transcription tools may help, but they don't touch the underlying problem. We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

Where in your organization is GenAI quietly making a symptom feel better while the real bottleneck stays put?

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

*Source: "family doctors still have to write up charts", "turned to GenAI transcription tools", "feel more productive without making a big difference", "we need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms."*

**Option B — measure outcome, not adoption**
📉 Canada has a real productivity problem, and we have for decades. In 1984 the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked; by 2022 it had fallen to 71%. The new national AI strategy promises to fix that with a 3 percent GDP boost by raising business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034.

Notice what's being measured: adoption. And adoption of AI doesn't make an organization more productive. Dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. Worse, a target built on an adoption rate invites AI washing, because when success is measured by how many organizations are "doing AI," they'll claim they are to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottleneck, and focus on eliminating that bottleneck. That's slower and less headline-friendly than an adoption target, and it's the only thing that actually moves the number.

What would it take for your organization to measure the outcome instead of the adoption rate?

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

*Source: "88% as productive... fallen to 71%", "adoption of AI doesn't make an organization more productive", "measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're doing AI", "look at each organization as a system... eliminating that bottleneck."*
